nodes.name: Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem
nodes.statement: The Bombieri--Vinogradov theorem \cite{bombieri1965large,vinogradov1965density} famously states that for any $x > 2$, $A > 0$, and $B$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{q \le x^{1/2}/(\log x)^B} \sup_{(a, q) = 1} \left\vert \pi(x; q, a) - \frac{\pi(x)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A}, \end{equation} where $\pi(x)$ denotes the number of primes up to $x$, and $\pi(x; q, a)$ denotes the number of these primes which are congruent to $a$ modulo $q$.
nodes.statement_short: Primes are equidistributed in APs on average over moduli up to $x^{1/2}/(\log x)^B$.
assumptions: for any $x > 2$, $A > 0$, and $B$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$
conclusions: \sum_{q \le x^{1/2}/(\log x)^B} \sup_{(a, q) = 1} \left\vert \pi(x; q, a) - \frac{\pi(x)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A},

nodes.name: Exponent of distribution
nodes.statement: We say that the primes have \emph{exponent of distribution} $\alpha < 1$ iff the analogue of \cref{eq:bv} holds true when summing over all moduli $q \le x^\alpha$.
differentia: the analogue of \cref{eq:bv} holds true when summing over all moduli $q \le x^\alpha$

nodes.name: Elliott–Halberstam conjecture
nodes.statement: The Elliott--Halberstam conjecture \cite{elliott1968conjecture} asserts that $\alpha = 1 - \varepsilon$ works for any $\varepsilon > 0$ (the implied constant depending on $\varepsilon$), but it remains open whether \cref{eq:bv} holds for any $\alpha > 1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: The primes have exponent of distribution $1-\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

nodes.name: y-smooth numbers S(x,y)
nodes.statement: In this paper, we are concerned with the case of \emph{$y$-smooth} (or \emph{$y$-friable}) numbers rather than primes; the objects of study here are the sets \[ S(x, y) := \{n \in \mathbf{Z}_+ : n \le x, \text{ and all prime factors of $n$ are $\le y$}\}, \] defined by two parameters $x, y \ge 2$, where $y$ will grow like $x^{o(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: $S(x,y)$ is the set of positive integers up to $x$ all of whose prime factors are at most $y$.

nodes.name: Smooth-number counting functions
nodes.statement: To state our main result, we denote \[ \begin{aligned} \Psi(x, y) &:= \# S(x, y), \\ \Psi_q(x, y) &:= \# \{n \in S(x, y) : (n, q) = 1\}, \\ \Psi(x, y; a, q) &:= \# \{n \in S(x, y) : n \equiv a \pmod{q}\}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Counts of $y$-smooth numbers up to $x$: all, coprime to $q$, and in the class $a$ mod $q$.

nodes.name: Smooth numbers in APs with moduli beyond $x^{3/5}$
nodes.statement: Let $a \in \mathbf{Z} \setminus \{0\}$ and $A, \varepsilon > 0$. Then there exists $C = C(A, \varepsilon) > 0$ such that in the range $x > 2$, $(\log x)^C \le y \le x^{1/C}$, one has \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{66/107-\varepsilon} \\ (q, a) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{a, A, \varepsilon} \frac{\Psi(x, y)}{(\log x)^A}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Smooth numbers are equidistributed in APs on average over moduli up to $x^{66/107-\varepsilon}$.
assumptions: in the range $x > 2$, $(\log x)^C \le y \le x^{1/C}$
conclusions: \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{66/107-\varepsilon} \\ (q, a) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{a, A, \varepsilon} \frac{\Psi(x, y)}{(\log x)^A}. \]
nodes.label: thm:distribution-simplified

nodes.name: Exceptional eigenvalues ($\theta_q$, $\theta_{\max}$)
nodes.statement: For $q \in \mathbf{Z}_+$, define $\theta_q := \sup_\lambda \sqrt{\max(0,1 - 4\lambda)}$, where $\lambda$ runs over all eigenvalues of the hyperbolic Laplacian for the Hecke congruence subgroup $\Gamma_0(q)$ (such $\lambda$ is called exceptional iff $\lambda < 1/4$). Also, let $\theta_{\max} := \sup_{q \ge 1} \theta_q$.
nodes.statement_short: $\theta_q$ measures exceptional Laplacian eigenvalues $\lambda<1/4$ for $\Gamma_0(q)$; $\theta_{\max}$ is its sup over $q$.
nodes.label: not:exceptional

nodes.name: Selberg eigenvalue conjecture
nodes.statement: One has $\theta_{\max} = 0$, i.e., there are no exceptional eigenvalues.
nodes.label: conj:selberg

nodes.name: Kim–Sarnak bound
nodes.statement: One has $\theta_{\max} \le 7/32$.
nodes.label: thm:kim-sarnak

nodes.name: Normalization of theta-parameters
nodes.statement: We warn the reader of another common normalization for the $\theta$-parameters, which differs by a factor of $2$ (resulting in a bound of $7/64$ in \cref{thm:kim-sarnak}); our normalization follows \cite{deshouillers1982kloosterman, maynard2020primes}. We give more details on the role of exceptional eigenvalues in our work in \cref{sec:deshouillers-iwaniec}.

nodes.name: Conditional exponent of distribution
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $C, \delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $x > 2$, $(\log x)^C \le y \le x^{1/C}$, and denote $u := (\log x)/(\log y)$, $H(u) := \exp \left(u \log^{-2} (u+1)\right)$. Then with an exponent of \begin{equation} \alpha := \frac{5-4\theta_{\max}}{8-6\theta_{\max}} - \varepsilon, \end{equation} one has \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{\alpha} \\ (q, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a_1 \overline{a_2}, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon, A} \Psi(x, y) \left(H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta}\right), \end{equation} for all $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbf{Z}$ with $1 \le |a_1|, |a_2| \le x^\delta$, and all $A \ge 0$. The implicit constant is effective if $A < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth numbers have exponent of distribution $(5-4\theta_{\max})/(8-6\theta_{\max})-\varepsilon$, uniformly in residues $a_1\overline{a_2}$.
assumptions: for all $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbf{Z}$ with $1 \le |a_1|, |a_2| \le x^\delta$, and all $A \ge 0$
conclusions: there exist $C, \delta > 0$ such that the following holds.

\sum_{\substack{q \le x^{\alpha} \\ (q, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a_1 \overline{a_2}, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon, A} \Psi(x, y) \left(H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta}\right),
The implicit constant is effective if $A < 1$.
nodes.label: thm:distribution

nodes.name: Meaning of the residue $a_1\overline{a_2}$
nodes.statement: In \cref{eq:exponent}, $\overline{a_2}$ denotes a multiplicative inverse of $a_2$ modulo $q$; so the residue $a_1\overline{a_2}$ corresponds to congruences of the form $a_2 n \equiv a_1 \pmod{q}$. The right-hand side of \cref{eq:exponent} is the same as in Drappeau's result \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}, and ultimately comes from a result of Harper (see \cref{lem:harper}).

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 1.1 from Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: In particular, \cref{conj:selberg} would imply an exponent of distribution of $5/8 - o(1)$, while \cref{thm:kim-sarnak} leads to the unconditional exponent of $66/107 - o(1)$ from \cref{thm:distribution-simplified}.
nodes.statement_short: Plug Kim–Sarnak's $\theta_{\max}\le 7/32$ into Theorem 1.4 to get exponent $66/107$.

nodes.name: Discrepancy $\Delta(f,x;q,a)$ and Siegel–Walfisz criterion
nodes.statement: We state a particular case of this result below, borrowing the notation \[ \Delta(f, x; q, a) := \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ n \equiv a \pmod{q}}} f(n) - \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ (n, q) = 1}} f(n) \] from \cite{drappeau2017smooth}; we also say that an arithmetic function $f$ satisifes the \emph{Siegel--Walfisz criterion} iff \[ \forall\ A > 0,\ (a, q) = 1,\ x \ge 2 : \qquad \Delta(f, x; q, a) \ll_A \frac{1}{(\log x)^A} \sum_{n \le x} |f(n)|. \]
nodes.statement_short: AP discrepancy of an arithmetic function $f$, and the Siegel–Walfisz criterion that it is small for every fixed power of log.

nodes.name: Smooth-supported multiplicative functions in APs
nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon, A > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $x > 2$, $x^\delta \ge y \ge \exp(\sqrt{\log x} \log \log x)$, and $f$ be a $1$-bounded completely multiplicative function supported on $y$-smooth integers, satisfying the Siegel--Walfisz criterion. Then for $\alpha := \frac{5-4\theta_{\max}}{8-6\theta_{\max}} - \varepsilon$, and all $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbf{Z}$ with $1 \le |a_1|, |a_2| \le x^{\delta}$, \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{\alpha} \\ (q, a_1a_2) = 1}} |\Delta(f, x; q, a_1 \overline{a_2})| \ll_{\varepsilon,A} \frac{\Psi(x, y)}{(\log x)^A}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Smooth-supported multiplicative functions satisfying Siegel–Walfisz are equidistributed in APs to moduli $x^{\alpha}$.
assumptions: $f$ be a $1$-bounded completely multiplicative function supported on $y$-smooth integers, satisfying the Siegel--Walfisz criterion
conclusions: \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{\alpha} \\ (q, a_1a_2) = 1}} |\Delta(f, x; q, a_1 \overline{a_2})| \ll_{\varepsilon,A} \frac{\Psi(x, y)}{(\log x)^A}.
nodes.label: thm:distribution-functions

nodes.name: Applications: smooth values of $n(n+1)$
nodes.statement: The improvement from $3/5-\varepsilon$ to the exponent in \cref{eq:exponent-theta} follows through in most applications of Drappeau's result \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}, such as \cite[Corollaire 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. Following \cite{de2020niveau}, our triple convolution estimate also implies a version of \cref{thm:distribution} restricted to smooth moduli, which can be used to deduce refined upper bounds for the number of smooth values assumed by a factorable quadratic polynomial. For instance, one has \[ \#\{n \sim x : n(n+1) \text{ is $y$-smooth} \} \ll_\varepsilon x \varrho(u)^{1+66/107-\varepsilon}, \] for $(\log x)^{O_\varepsilon(1)} \le y \le x$, where $u = (\log x)/(\log y)$ and $\varrho(u)$ is the Dickman function (satisfying $\Psi(x, y) = x \varrho(u) e^{O_\varepsilon(u)}$ in this range \cite{de2020niveau,hildebrand1986number}).
nodes.statement_short: The improvement carries over to applications, e.g. a bound for $n\sim x$ with $n(n+1)$ $y$-smooth.

nodes.name: Sketch of the argument for Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement:
Let us give a very rough sketch of our argument, for a simpler case of \cref{thm:distribution-simplified}. Consider the residue $a = 1$, the smoothness parameter $y = x^{1/\sqrt{\log \log x}}$, and a sum over moduli just above the $3/5$ threshold, say \[ r \le R := x^{3/5 + \sigma}, \] for some small $\sigma \gg 1$ (we switch the variable $q$ to $r$, following \cite{drappeau2015theoremes,drappeau2017smooth}). Using the factorization properties of smooth numbers, it suffices to prove a triple convolution estimate roughly of the form  egin{equation} \sum_{r \sim R} ho_r \sum_{m \sim M} \alpha_m \sum_{n \sim N}  eta_n \sum_{\ell \sim L} \gamma_\ell \left(1_{mn\ell \equiv 1 \pmod{r}} -  rac{\mathbbm{1}_{(mn\ell, r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} ight) \ll_A  rac{x}{(\log x)^A}, \end{equation} where $(ho_r)$, $(\alpha_m)$, $( eta_n)$, $(\gamma_\ell)$ are arbitrary $1$-bounded complex sequences, but we are free to choose the parameters $M, N, L \gg 1$ subject to $MNL \asymp x$. We pick  egin{equation} M :=  rac{x^{1-\delta}}{R}, \qquad\qquad N :=  rac{x^{1-2\delta}}{R}, \qquad\qquad L :=  rac{R^2}{x^{1-3\delta}}, \end{equation} for some small $\delta = o(1)$; thus $M, N \approx x^{2/5-\sigma}$ and $L \approx x^{1/5+2\sigma}$. Note additionally that $NL = x^{\delta} R$. \subsection{Limitations of previous approaches} Following previous works \cite{bombieri1986primes,drappeau2015theoremes,maynard2020primes} based on the \emph{dispersion method}, we apply Cauchy--Schwarz in the $r, m$ variables, expand the square, and Fourier-complete the resulting sums in $m$ to sums over $h$. Ignoring GCD-constraints, the key resulting exponential sum is a smoothed variant of  egin{equation} \sum_{r \sim R}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N}  eta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{r}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} 	extnormal{e}\left(h  rac{\overline{k}}{r} ight), \end{equation} where $(u_k)$ is the convolution of the original sequences $( eta_n)$, $(\gamma_\ell)$. We flip moduli in the exponential via Bezout's identity, and substitute $t := (k - n\ell)/r$ to reduce to sums of the form \[ \sum_{t \sim x^\delta}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N}  eta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{t}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} 	extnormal{e}\left(h t  rac{\overline{n\ell}}{k} ight). \] Following Maynard \cite{maynard2020primes}, we apply Cauchy--Schwarz in the $t, n, k$ variables (keeping the congruence modulo $t$ inside), and expand the square to reach the sum \[ \sum_{t \sim x^\delta} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ell_2 \sim L \ \ell_1 \equiv \ell_2 \pmod{t}}} \gamma_{\ell_1} \overline{\gamma_{\ell_2}} \sum_{h_1, h_2 \sim R/M} \sum_{k \sim NL} \sum_{\substack{n \sim N \ n \equiv k\overline{\ell_1} \pmod{t}}} 	extnormal{e}\left(t(h_1 \ell_2 - h_2 \ell_1)  rac{\overline{n\ell_1\ell_2}}{k} ight), \] which we ultimately need to bound by $\ll_A RNL^2 (\log x)^{-A}$; note that the trivial bound is larger by about $(R/M)^2$, due to the sum over $h_1, h_2$ introduced by Poisson summation. We bound the contribution of the diagonal terms (with $h_1\ell_2 = h_2\ell_1$) by  egin{equation} \sum_{t \sim x^\delta}\, \sum_{\ell_1 \sim L}\, \sum_{h_2 \sim R/M} x^{o(1)} \sum_{k \sim NL} \sum_{\substack{n \sim N \ n \equiv k\overline{\ell_1} \pmod{t}}} 1 \ll x^{o(1)} RNL^2  rac{N}{M}, \end{equation} which is acceptable since $N/M = x^{-\delta}$. We then introduce Kloosterman sums $S(i, j; k)$ by completing the sum in $n$ to a sum over $j$, and find acceptable contributions from the zeroth Fourier coefficient ($j = 0$), as well as from the terms with $\ell_1 = \ell_2$; here it suffices to use the Weil bound, respectively an estimate of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite[Theorem 9]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}. It ultimately remains to bound a variant of  egin{equation} \sum_{t \sim x^\delta} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ell_2 \sim L \ \ell_1 \equiv \ell_2 \pmod{t} \ \ell_1 
eq \ell_2}} \sum_{\substack{h_1, h_2 \sim R/M \ h_1\ell_2 
eq h_2\ell_1}} \left\vert \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} 	extnormal{e}\left( rac{j\overline{\ell_1}}{t}ight) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left((h_1\ell_2 - h_2\ell_1)\overline{\ell_1\ell_2}, j; kight)ight\vert, \end{equation} by $\ll_A N^2 L^4 (\log x)^{-A}$. Inserting $1$-bounded coefficients $\xi_{h_1, h_2}$ (also depending on $t, \ell_1, \ell_2, \omega$), and letting $a_d := \sum_{h_1 \ell_2 - h_2 \ell_1 = d} \xi_{h_1, h_2}$, the sum over $h_1, h_2$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} roughly reduces to  egin{equation} \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_d \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} 	extnormal{e}\left( rac{j\overline{\ell_1}}{t}ight) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; kight). \end{equation} Such sums can be bounded using the spectral theory of automorphic forms, specifically through the aforementioned work of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite{deshouillers1982kloosterman} (based on the Kuznetsov trace formula and the Weil bound); the relevant \emph{level} of the congruence group in \cref{not:exceptional} is $Q = \ell_1\ell_2$. Indeed, Maynard \cite{maynard2020primes} uses \cite[Theorem 9]{deshouillers1982kloosterman} to bound (a smoothed variant of) the sum in \cref{eq:sketch-kloosterman} by \[ x^{	heta_Q/2 + o(1)} NL^{5/2} \left(\sum_{d \sim RL/M} |a_d|^2ight)^{1/2}, \] and consequently the sum in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} by  egin{equation} x^{	heta_{\max}/2 + o(1)} NL^{5/2}  rac{R^{3/2}L^{3/2}}{M^{3/2}} \approx x^{(	heta_{\max}+3)/2 + 10\sigma}. \end{equation} Unfortunately, this falls short of the desired bound of $N^2 L^4 (\log x)^{-A} \approx x^{8/5 + 6\sigma}$, unless  egin{equation} 4\sigma <  rac{1}{10} -  rac{	heta_{\max}}{2}. \end{equation} This is (barely) impossible with the currently best-known bound of $	heta_{\max}/2 \le 7/64 \approx 0.109$. \subsection{Improved exponential sum manipulations for specific ranges} Starting from the work of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, better bounds (in the $	heta$-aspect) for sums like \cref{eq:sketch-kloosterman} have been available when one additionally averages over the level $\ell_1\ell_2$, and at least one of the sequences of coefficients is independent of the level. Indeed, Drappeau's triple convolution estimate \cite{drappeau2015theoremes} and prior works rely on \cite[Theorem 12]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, which gives such a result for incomplete Kloosterman sums. Following Maynard's argument (which is in turn based on Bombieri--Friedlander--Iwaniec's work in \cite[\S 10]{bombieri1987primes2}), we prefer to complete our Kloosterman sums, bound the contribution from the zeroth Fourier coefficient by hand, and separate into terms with $\ell_1 = \ell_2$ and $\ell_1 
eq \ell_2$, all before invoking Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds. We then aim to apply an optimized bound for sums of complete Kloosterman sums with averaging over the level (given in \cref{thm:di-type-bound}), which improves \cite[Theorem 11]{deshouillers1982kloosterman} by making the dependence on the $	heta_{\max}$ parameter explicit. But for this strategy to work out, we would need:  egin{itemize} \item[(1).] The range of $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} to be (discretely) dense inside $[L, 2L]^2$, and \item[(2).] Crucially, the coefficients $e\left(j \overline{\ell_1} / t ight)$ to not depend on $\ell_1, \ell_2$. \end{itemize} While (2) is obviously false in our case, it is only barely false for the specific ranges in \cref{eq:sketch-ranges}, due to the smallness of the parameter $t \sim x^\delta$. In particular, losing a factor of at most $x^{O(\delta)} = x^{o(1)}$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum}, we may fix $t$ and the values of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2 \pmod{t}$, turning (2) into a true statement at the expense of (1). The number of pairs $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ now becomes $\asymp L^2/t^2$, which ends up costing us another acceptable factor of $x^{o(1)}$. Overall, it remains to bound a sum of the form  egin{equation} \sum_{\ell_1,\ell_2 \sim L}\, \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_{d,\ell_1,\ell_2} \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} 	extnormal{e}\left(j\omegaight) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; kight), \end{equation} for some fixed $\omega \in \mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$ (independent of $\ell_1, \ell_2$). Using \cref{thm:di-type-bound}, we obtain a bound like \cref{eq:sketch-final-bound} where the factor depending on $	heta_{\max}$ is \[ \left( rac{NL}{L^2}ight)^{	heta_{\max}} \approx x^{\left( rac{1}{5}-3\sigmaight) 	heta_{\max}}, \] rather than $x^{	heta_{\max}/2}$. Thus instead of \cref{eq:sketch-sigma}, we now reach the desired bound provided that \[ \left(4 - 3	heta_{\max}ight)\sigma <  rac{1}{10} -  rac{	heta_{\max}}{5}, \] which is possible since $(1/5) \cdot (7/32) = 0.04375 < 0.1$. In fact, this handles all values \[ \sigma <  rac{1-2	heta_{\max}}{40-30	heta_{\max}} \qquad\qquad \iff \qquad\qquad  rac{3}{5} + \sigma <  rac{5-4	heta_{\max}}{8-6	heta_{\max}}, \] reaching the exponent of distribution in \cref{eq:exponent-theta}. Plugging in Kim--Sarnak's bound of $	heta_{\max} \le 7/32$ (\cref{thm:kim-sarnak}) yields the unconditional exponent of $66/107 \approx 0.617$ from \cref{thm:distribution-simplified}.  egin{remark} It is likely that optimized Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds like \cref{thm:di-kloosterman} could also improve Drappeau's argument \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}, leading to a triple convolution estimate with different ranges than in our \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}. In terms of the final exponent of distribution of smooth numbers, all such methods currently seem limited below $66/107$ unconditionally (and $5/8$ conditionally). \end{remark} \subsection{Completing the argument} To increase the range of uniformity in $y$, we adapt Drappeau's version of the dispersion method \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}: we aim for a triple convolution estimate with a power-saving in \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}, after separating the contribution of small-conductor Dirichlet characters \[  rac{1}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{r} \ 	extnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\varepsilon}} \chi(mn\ell) \] from \cref{eq:sketch-triple-conv}; this can be handled via \cref{lem:harper}. As a result, the simpler two dispersion sums $\mathcal{S}_2$, $\mathcal{S}_3$ and their main terms involve Dirichlet characters (see \cref{prop:setup,prop:main-terms}), which ultimately bring in the classical Gauss sum bound (\cref{lem:gauss}) and the multiplicative large sieve (\cref{lem:large-sieve}). The difficulties in working with a general residue $a_1 \overline{a_2}$ for $a_1, a_2 \ll x^\delta$, and in obtaining power savings throughout the computations in \cref{subsec:limitations}, are quite tedious but purely technical (following \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}). We also adapt a ``deamplification'' argument of Maynard \cite{maynard2020primes}, which introduces an artificial sum over $e \sim E = x^{o(1)}$ into the dispersion sums (by averaging over the residue of $n\ell \pmod{e}$ before applying Cauchy--Schwarz); for instance, the sum in \cref{eq:sketch-main-exponential} becomes \[ \sum_{e \sim E}\, \sum_{r \sim R}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N}  eta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{re}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} 	extnormal{e}\left(h  rac{\overline{k}}{r} ight). \] Keeping $e$ inside the second application of Cauchy--Schwarz, this essentially reduces the contribution of the diagonal terms in \cref{eq:sketch-diagonal-terms} by a factor of $E$, allowing us to cover wider ranges of sequence lengths in \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} (including the case $M = N$). This is generally convenient, and critical when one has less control over the sizes of the sequence lengths (which is the case in applications to the primes, but not to smooth numbers).
nodes.statement_short: Dispersion method, Poisson summation, Maynard's Cauchy–Schwarz arrangement and Kloosterman sums. Fixing $t$ and $\ell_i$ mod $t$ makes coefficients level-independent, so an optimized Deshouillers–Iwaniec bound with level averaging applies.

nodes.name: Possible improvement of Drappeau's argument
nodes.statement: It is likely that optimized Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds like \cref{thm:di-kloosterman} could also improve Drappeau's argument \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}, leading to a triple convolution estimate with different ranges than in our \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}. In terms of the final exponent of distribution of smooth numbers, all such methods currently seem limited below $66/107$ unconditionally (and $5/8$ conditionally).
nodes.section: 2.2 Improved exponential sum manipulations for specific ranges

nodes.name: Big-O and Vinogradov notation
nodes.statement: We use the standard asymptotic notation in analytic number theory, with $f = O(g)$ (or $f \ll g$) meaning that there exists some constant $C > 0$ such that $|f| \le Cg$ globally.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence notation
nodes.statement: We write $f \asymp g$ when $f \ll g$ and $g \ll f$, and indicate that the implied constants may depend on a parameter $\varepsilon$ by placing it in the subscript (e.g., $f = O_\varepsilon(g)$, $f \ll_\varepsilon g$, $f \asymp_\varepsilon g$).

nodes.name: Little-o notation
nodes.statement: We also say that $f = o(g) = o_{x \to \infty}(g)$ if and only if $f(x)/g(x) \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$.

nodes.name: L^q and l^q norms
nodes.statement: Given $q \in [1, \infty]$, we write $||f||_q$ for the $L^q$ norm of a measurable function $f : \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{C}$ (using the Lebesgue measure), and $||a_n||_q$ for the $\ell^q$ norm of a complex sequence $(a_n)$.

nodes.name: Number sets and additive character e(x)
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathbf{Z}_+, \mathbf{Z}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{H}$ the sets of positive integers, integers, real numbers, complex numbers, and complex numbers with positive imaginary part respectively, and set $\textnormal{e}(x) := \exp(2 \pi i x)$ for $x \in \mathbf{R}$ (or $x \in \mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$).

nodes.name: Residue rings and modular inverse
nodes.statement: We write $\mathbf{Z}/n\mathbf{Z}$ and $(\mathbf{Z}/n\mathbf{Z})^\times$ for the additive and multiplicative groups modulo a positive integer $n$, and denote the inverse of $c \in (\mathbf{Z}/n\mathbf{Z})^\times$ by $\overline{c}$.

nodes.name: Dyadic notation n ~ N
nodes.statement: Given $N > 0$, we write $n \sim N$ for the statement that $N < n \le 2N$, usually in the subscripts of sums.

nodes.name: Indicator notation
nodes.statement: Given a statement $S$, we write $\mathbbm{1}_S$ for its truth value (e.g., $\mathbbm{1}_{2 \mid n}$ equals $1$ when $n$ is even and $0$ otherwise); we may use the same notation for the indicator function of a set $S$ (i.e., $\mathbbm{1}_S(x) = \mathbbm{1}_{x \in S}$).

nodes.name: gcd and lcm notation
nodes.statement: Given $a_1, \ldots, a_k \in \mathbf{Z}$, we write $(a_1, \ldots, a_k)$ (if not all $a_i$ are $0$) and $[a_1, \ldots, a_k]$ (if none of the $a_i$ are $0$) for their greatest common divisor and lowest common multiple, among the positive integers.

nodes.name: Radical and b-infinity divisibility
nodes.statement: Given $a \in \mathbf{Z} \setminus \{0\}$, we write $\textnormal{rad}(a)$ for the largest square-free positive integer dividing $a$; for $b \in \mathbf{Z}$, we also write $a \mid b^\infty$ if and only if $\textnormal{rad}(a) \mid b$ (i.e., $a$ divides a large enough power of $b$), and $(a, b^\infty)$ for the greatest divisor of $a$ whose prime factors divide $b$.

nodes.name: Möbius, divisor and totient functions
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mu$, $\tau$ and $\varphi$ the M\"obius function, the divisor-counting function ($\tau(n) := \sum_{d \mid n} 1$) and the Euler totient function ($\varphi(n) := \sum_{1 \le a \le n} \mathbbm{1}_{(a, n) = 1}$).

nodes.name: Classical divisor and totient bounds
nodes.statement: We may use various classical bounds involving these functions implicitly, including the divisor bound $\tau(n) \ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon$ (valid for all $\varepsilon > 0$), the lower bound $\varphi(n) \gg n/(\log \log n)$, and the upper bounds \[ \sum_{n \sim N} \frac{1}{\varphi(n)} \ll 1, \qquad\qquad \sum_{n \le x} \frac{\tau(n)}{\varphi(n)} \ll (\log x)^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Divisor bound $\tau(n)\ll n^{\varepsilon}$, $\varphi(n)\gg n/\log\log n$, and averages of $1/\varphi$ and $\tau/\varphi$.

nodes.name: Proof of the averaged totient bound
nodes.statement: (The latter follows from the former, using that $\varphi(ab) \gg \varphi(a) \varphi(b)$ for positive integers $a, b$.)
nodes.statement_short: Deduce the $\tau/\varphi$ average from the $1/\varphi$ average via $\varphi(ab)\gg\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet characters, conductor, primitivity
nodes.statement: We write $\chi \pmod{q}$ to indicate that $\chi$ is a Dirichlet character with period $q$ (of which there are $\varphi(q)$), and denote by $\textnormal{cond}(\chi)$ the conductor of $\chi$ (which divides $q$; this is the smallest positive integer $d$ such that there exists a Dirichlet character $\chi' \pmod{d}$ with $\chi(n) = \chi'(n) \mathbbm{1}_{(n, q) = 1}$ for all $n \in \mathbf{Z}$); we say that $\chi \pmod{q}$ is \emph{primitive} when $\textnormal{cond}(\chi) = q$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for Dirichlet characters mod $q$, their conductor, and primitivity.

nodes.name: Bézout's identity
nodes.statement: For any relatively prime integers $a, b$, one has \[ \frac{1}{ab} \equiv \frac{\overline{a}}{b} + \frac{\overline{b}}{a} \quad \pmod{1}. \]
assumptions: For any relatively prime integers $a, b$
nodes.label: lem:bezout

nodes.name: Proof of Bézout's identity
nodes.statement: Note that here, $\overline{a}$ and $\overline{b}$ denote the inverses of $a$ and $b$ modulo $b$ and $a$ respectively, so we have $a \overline{a} \equiv 1 \pmod{b}$ and $b \overline{b} \equiv 1 \pmod{a}$. The conclusion follows from the Chinese remainder theorem, once we multiply the congruence by $ab$ and verify it modulo $a$ and $b$ separately.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $ab$ and verify the congruence modulo $a$ and $b$ separately via CRT.

nodes.name: Contribution of small-conductor characters
nodes.statement: There exist constants $\varepsilon, \delta, C > 0$ such that for $(\log x)^C \le y \le x$, $Q \le x$ and $A > 0$, one has \[ \sum_{q \le Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{q} \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\varepsilon}} \left\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \chi(n) \right\vert \ll_A \Psi(x, y) \left(H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta} \right), \] where $u := (\log x)/(\log y)$. The implicit constant is effective if $A < 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-trivial characters of small conductor have small sums over smooth numbers, on average over moduli.
assumptions: for $(\log x)^C \le y \le x$, $Q \le x$ and $A > 0$
conclusions: \sum_{q \le Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{q} \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\varepsilon}} \left\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \chi(n) \right\vert \ll_A \Psi(x, y) \left(H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta} \right),
The implicit constant is effective if $A < 1$.
nodes.label: lem:harper

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2 (citation)
nodes.statement: This is the same as \cite[Lemme 5]{drappeau2015theoremes}, and follows from the work of Harper in \cite[\S 3.3]{harper2012bombieri}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Drappeau's Lemme 5, based on Harper's work.

nodes.name: Trivial character excluded
nodes.statement: The condition $\textnormal{cond}(\chi) > 1$ in \cref{lem:harper} leaves out the trivial character $\chi_0$.

nodes.name: Multiplicative large sieve
nodes.statement: For $Q, M, N \ge 1$ and any sequence $(a_n)$ of complex numbers, one has \[ \sum_{q \le Q} \frac{q}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{q} \\ \chi \textnormal{ primitive}}} \left\vert \sum_{M < n \le M+N} a_n \chi(n) \right\vert^2 \le (N + Q^2 - 1) \sum_{M < n \le M+N} |a_n|^2. \]
assumptions: For $Q, M, N \ge 1$ and any sequence $(a_n)$ of complex numbers
conclusions: \sum_{q \le Q} \frac{q}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{q} \\ \chi \textnormal{ primitive}}} \left\vert \sum_{M < n \le M+N} a_n \chi(n) \right\vert^2 \le (N + Q^2 - 1) \sum_{M < n \le M+N} |a_n|^2.
nodes.label: lem:large-sieve

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3 (citation)
nodes.statement: See, for example, \cite[Theorem 7.13]{iwaniec2021analytic}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Iwaniec–Kowalski.

nodes.name: Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Given an integrable function $f : \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{C}$, we write \[ \widehat{f}(\xi) := \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t)\, \textnormal{e}(-\xi t)\ dt \] for its Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Truncated Poisson summation
nodes.statement: Let $C > 0$, $x > 1$, $1 < M \ll x$, and $\Phi : \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{R}$ be a smooth function supported in $[1/10, 10]$ such that $||\Phi^{(j)}||_\infty \ll_j (\log x)^{jC}$ for $j \ge 0$. Then for all positive integers $q \ll x$, any $a \in \mathbf{Z}/q\mathbf{Z}$, and any $\varepsilon > 0$, $H \ge x^{\varepsilon} qM^{-1}$, one has \[ \sum_{m \equiv a \pmod{q}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) = \frac{M}{q} \sum_{|h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi} \left(\frac{hM}{q} \right) \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{ah}{q}\right) + O_{\varepsilon,C}\left(x^{-100}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: A smooth sum over an AP mod $q$ equals its Fourier expansion truncated at $|h|\le H$, up to $O(x^{-100})$.
assumptions: $\Phi : \mathbf{R} \to \mathbf{R}$ be a smooth function supported in $[1/10, 10]$ such that $||\Phi^{(j)}||_\infty \ll_j (\log x)^{jC}$ for $j \ge 0$
all positive integers $q \ll x$, any $a \in \mathbf{Z}/q\mathbf{Z}$, and any $\varepsilon > 0$, $H \ge x^{\varepsilon} qM^{-1}$
nodes.label: lem:poisson

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4 (citation)
nodes.statement: This is the same as \cite[Lemma 13.4]{maynard2020primes} (see also \cite[Lemme 2]{drappeau2015theoremes}).
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Maynard (Lemma 13.4).

nodes.name: Kloosterman sum
nodes.statement: While \cref{lem:poisson} will introduce exponential sums into our estimates, we will need an additional corollary (and generalization) of it to obtain sums of complete \emph{Kloosterman sums}, defined by \[ S(m, n; c) := \sum_{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/c\mathbf{Z})^\times} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{mb + n\overline{b}}{c}\right), \qquad\qquad c \in \mathbf{Z}_+,\ m, n \in \mathbf{Z} \textnormal{ (or $\mathbf{Z}/c\mathbf{Z}$)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Complete Kloosterman sum $S(m,n;c)=\sum_{b} e((mb+n\bar b)/c)$.

nodes.name: Kloosterman completion
nodes.statement: Let $C, x, M, \Phi$ be as in \cref{lem:poisson}. Then for all positive integers $c, q \ll x$ with $(c, q) = 1$, any $a \in \mathbf{Z}/q\mathbf{Z}$, $n \in \mathbf{Z}/c\mathbf{Z}$, and any $\varepsilon > 0$, $H \ge x^\varepsilon cq M^{-1}$, one has \[ \sum_{\substack{m \equiv a \pmod{q} \\ (m, c) = 1}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{\overline{m}n}{c}\right) = \frac{M}{cq} \sum_{|h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{cq}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{ah \overline{c}}{q}\right) S(h\overline{q}, n; c) + O_{\varepsilon, C}\left(x^{-100}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Smooth sums of $e(\bar m n/c)$ over an AP complete to sums of Kloosterman sums $S(h\bar q,n;c)$.
assumptions: Let $C, x, M, \Phi$ be as in \cref{lem:poisson}
all positive integers $c, q \ll x$ with $(c, q) = 1$, any $a \in \mathbf{Z}/q\mathbf{Z}$, $n \in \mathbf{Z}/c\mathbf{Z}$, and any $\varepsilon > 0$, $H \ge x^\varepsilon cq M^{-1}$
conclusions: \sum_{\substack{m \equiv a \pmod{q} \\ (m, c) = 1}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{\overline{m}n}{c}\right) = \frac{M}{cq} \sum_{|h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{cq}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{ah \overline{c}}{q}\right) S(h\overline{q}, n; c) + O_{\varepsilon, C}\left(x^{-100}\right).
nodes.label: lem:completion

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: Rewrite the left-hand side as \[ \sum_{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/c\mathbf{Z})^\times} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{\overline{b} n}{c} \right) \sum_{\substack{m \equiv a \pmod{q} \\ m \equiv b \pmod{c}}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right), \] and apply \cref{lem:poisson} to expand the inner summation, for the unique residue class $r \in \mathbf{Z}/cq\mathbf{Z}$ which is congruent to $a \pmod{q}$ and to $b \pmod{c}$ (invoking the Chinese remainder theorem). Noting that \[ \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{rh}{cq}\right) = \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{rh \overline{c}}{q} + \frac{rh \overline{q}}{c}\right) = \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{ah \overline{c}}{q} + \frac{bh \overline{q}}{c}\right) \] by \cref{lem:bezout}, swapping sums and taking out the factor depending on $a$, the conclusion follows.
nodes.statement_short: Split $m$ by residue mod $c$, apply truncated Poisson mod $cq$ and separate phases by Bézout.

nodes.name: Gauss sum bound
nodes.statement: For any $a \in \mathbf{Z}$, $q \in \mathbf{Z}_+$, and Dirichlet character $\chi \pmod{q}$, one has \[ \left\vert \sum_{b \in \mathbf{Z}/q\mathbf{Z}} \chi(b)\ \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{ab}{q}\right) \right\vert \le \textnormal{cond}(\chi)^{1/2} \sum_{d \mid (a, q)} d. \]
nodes.label: lem:gauss

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6 (citation)
nodes.statement: This follows from \cite[Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2]{iwaniec2021analytic}, and is also used in \cite[\S 3.2]{drappeau2015theoremes}.
nodes.statement_short: Cited from Iwaniec–Kowalski.

nodes.name: Weil–Ramanujan bound
nodes.statement: For $c \in \mathbf{Z}_+$ and $m, n \in \mathbf{Z}$ (or $\mathbf{Z}/c\mathbf{Z}$), one has \[ S(m, n; c) \ll \tau(c)\, (m, n, c)^{1/2} c^{1/2}. \] For $m = 0$, we have in fact $|S(0, n; c)| \le (n, c)$.
nodes.label: lem:weil

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7 (citation)
nodes.statement: The first (Weil) bound is \cite[Corollary 11.12]{iwaniec2021analytic}, while the second (Ramanujan) bound can be deduced by M\"obius inversion.
nodes.statement_short: Weil bound cited; Ramanujan bound by Möbius inversion.

nodes.name: Incomplete Weil bound
nodes.statement: Let $x > 1$, $1 < M \ll x$, and let $n, c, k, \ell \ll x$ be positive integers. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$, one has \[ \sum_{\substack{(m, ck) = 1 \\ \ell \mid m \le M}} \frac{m}{\varphi(m)} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{\overline{m}n}{c}\right) \ll_{\varepsilon} x^\varepsilon \left((n, c)^{1/2} c^{1/2} + \frac{(n, c)}{\ell c} M \right). \]
assumptions: Let $x > 1$, $1 < M \ll x$, and let $n, c, k, \ell \ll x$ be positive integers
conclusions: \sum_{\substack{(m, ck) = 1 \\ \ell \mid m \le M}} \frac{m}{\varphi(m)} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{\overline{m}n}{c}\right) \ll_{\varepsilon} x^\varepsilon \left((n, c)^{1/2} c^{1/2} + \frac{(n, c)}{\ell c} M \right).
nodes.label: lem:incomplete-weil

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.8
nodes.statement: This follows immediately from \cite[(2.5)]{drappeau2015theoremes} and the divisor bound (see also \cite[Lemme 4]{fouvry1982repartition} and \cite[Lemma 16.1]{maynard2020primes}). It can be proven by expanding $m\varphi(m)^{-1} = \sum_{v \mid m^\infty} v^{-1}$ and $\mathbbm{1}_{(m, k)} = \sum_{d \mid k} \mu(d) \mathbbm{1}_{d \mid m}$, changing variables $m \gets m [\ell, \textnormal{rad}(v), d]$, completing sums via a result like \cref{lem:completion}, and finally applying \cref{lem:weil} for the terms $h = 0$ and $h \neq 0$ separately.
nodes.statement_short: Cited; alternatively expand $m/\varphi(m)$ and coprimality, complete sums and apply the Weil bound.

nodes.name: DI-type Kloosterman bound
nodes.statement: Let $1 \ll M, N, R, S, C \ll x^{O(1)}$, $(a_{m,r,s})$ be a complex sequence supported in $m \sim M, r \sim R, s \sim S$, and $\omega \in \mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$. Also, let $g(t)$ be a smooth function supported on $t \asymp 1$, with bounded derivatives $||g^{(j)}||_\infty \ll_{j} 1$ for $j \ge 0$. Then for any $\eta > 0$, one has \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{m \sim M} a_{m,r,s} \sum_{n \sim N} \textnormal{e}(n\omega) \sum_{(c, r) = 1} g\left(\frac{c}{C}\right)\, S(m\overline{r}, \pm n; sc) \ll_\eta x^\eta\, \left(1 + \frac{C}{R\sqrt{S}}\right)^{\theta_{\max}}\, ||a_{m,r,s}||_2 \\ \times \sqrt{NRS} \left(\frac{C^2}{R} (M + RS)(N + RS) + MN \right)^{1/2}, \end{aligned} \] where we recall that $\theta_{\max} \le 7/32$ by \cref{thm:kim-sarnak}. (The `$\pm n$' notation indicates that either consistent choice of sign is allowable.)
nodes.statement_short: Bound for sums of Kloosterman sums with level averaging, with exceptional-eigenvalue loss $(1+C/(R\sqrt S))^{\theta_{\max}}$.
assumptions: Let $1 \ll M, N, R, S, C \ll x^{O(1)}$
$(a_{m,r,s})$ be a complex sequence supported in $m \sim M, r \sim R, s \sim S$
let $g(t)$ be a smooth function supported on $t \asymp 1$, with bounded derivatives $||g^{(j)}||_\infty \ll_{j} 1$ for $j \ge 0$
conclusions: \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{m \sim M} a_{m,r,s} \sum_{n \sim N} \textnormal{e}(n\omega) \sum_{(c, r) = 1} g\left(\frac{c}{C}\right)\, S(m\overline{r}, \pm n; sc) \ll_\eta x^\eta\, \left(1 + \frac{C}{R\sqrt{S}}\right)^{\theta_{\max}}\, ||a_{m,r,s}||_2 \\ \times \sqrt{NRS} \left(\frac{C^2}{R} (M + RS)(N + RS) + MN \right)^{1/2}, \end{aligned} \]
nodes.label: thm:di-type-bound

nodes.name: Smooth numbers versus primes: factorization flexibility
nodes.statement: One can apply the most efficient convolution estimates directly to the setting of smooth numbers (and smooth-supported multiplicative functions), since these can essentially be factorized into any number of factors of pre-specified sizes. By contrast, in the case of primes, combinatorial decompositions of the von--Mangoldt function produce more types of convolution sums, requiring different estimates for distinct ranges (typically organized into `Type I' and `Type II' information).

nodes.name: Character partial sum $\omega_D$ and error term $\mathcal{E}_D$
nodes.statement: Drappeau \cite{drappeau2015theoremes,drappeau2017smooth} noticed that since \[ \mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv 1 \mod{r}} = \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\chi \pmod{r}} \chi(k) = \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(k, r) = 1}}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k), \] one can instead consider the partial sum \begin{equation} \omega_D(k; r) := \sum_{\substack{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k), \qquad\quad \text{where} \qquad\quad \mathcal{X}_D := \{\chi \text{ primitive} : \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le D\}, \end{equation} and work with the error term \[ \mathcal{E}_D(k; r) := \mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv 1 \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(k,r) = 1}}{\varphi(r)} \omega_D(k; r) \ = \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(k,r) = 1}}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{r} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D}} \chi(k). \]
nodes.statement_short: $\omega_D$ sums primitive characters of conductor $\le D$ dividing $r$; $\mathcal{E}_D$ is the resulting approximation error to $1_{k\equiv1 (r)}$.

nodes.name: Crude bound for $\omega_D$
nodes.statement: We also note the crude bound \[ |\omega_D(k; r)| \le |\mathcal{X}(D)| \le D^2, \] which may be used implicitly in our proofs.

nodes.name: Triple convolution estimate
nodes.statement: For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $a_1, a_2$ be coprime nonzero integers, and let $M, N, L, x > 2$ satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} a_1, a_2 \ll x^\delta, \qquad MNL \asymp x, \qquad\quad x^{(1-\varepsilon)/2} \ll R \ll x^{-5\varepsilon} NL \ll x^{(2/3) - 11\varepsilon}, \qquad N^9 L^8 \ll x^3 R^4, \\ N \ll \frac{x^{1-2\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad N^4 L^7 \max(1, N/L)^{2\theta} \ll x^{2-16\varepsilon}R^2, \qquad N^{12-6\theta} L^{11-6\theta} \ll x^{6-4(\theta+\varepsilon)} R^2, \end{gathered} \end{equation} for $\theta = \theta_{\max}$. Then for any $1$-bounded complex sequences $(\alpha_m)$, $(\beta_n)$, $(\gamma_\ell)$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \sum_{m \sim M} \sum_{n \sim N} \sum_{\ell \sim L} \alpha_m \beta_n \gamma_\ell\, \mathcal{E}_D(mn\ell \overline{a_1} a_2; r) \right\vert \ll_\varepsilon \frac{x (\log x)^4}{\min\left(x^\delta, \sqrt{D}\right)}, \end{equation} for all $1 \le D \le x^\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Triple convolutions $\alpha*\beta*\gamma$ are equidistributed in APs to moduli $R$ beyond $x^{3/5}$, with a power saving up to small-conductor characters.
assumptions: Let $a_1, a_2$ be coprime nonzero integers
conclusions: there exists $\delta > 0$ such that the following holds.

\sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \sum_{m \sim M} \sum_{n \sim N} \sum_{\ell \sim L} \alpha_m \beta_n \gamma_\ell\, \mathcal{E}_D(mn\ell \overline{a_1} a_2; r) \right\vert \ll_\varepsilon \frac{x (\log x)^4}{\min\left(x^\delta, \sqrt{D}\right)},
nodes.label: thm:triple-conv-estimate

nodes.name: Power saving in the triple convolution estimate
nodes.statement: Error terms of the form $O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\delta})$ are dominated by the right-hand side of \cref{eq:triple-conv-estimate}, and will be available throughout most of our proof. If $x^{2\delta} \le D \le x^\varepsilon$, then the right-hand side of \cref{eq:triple-conv-estimate} becomes $x^{1-\delta} (\log x)^4$, i.e., a power-saving; having an explicit dependence on the conductor bound $D$ is required for the application to smooth-supported multiplicative functions, as in \cite{drappeau2017smooth}.

nodes.name: Optimal parameter choice
nodes.statement: If one is free to choose the parameters $M$, $N$, $L$ subject only to the constraints in \cref{eq:conditions} and $MNL \asymp x$, then in order to maximize the range $R$, it is optimal to pick (up to $x^{o(1)}$ factors) \begin{equation} R \approx x^{(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta)}, \qquad\quad M \approx \frac{x}{R}, \qquad\quad N \approx \frac{x}{R}, \qquad\quad L \approx \frac{R^2}{x}. \end{equation} This improves on the conditions from Drappeau's triple convolution estimate \cite[(3.2)]{drappeau2015theoremes}, which can handle moduli up to $R \approx x^{3/5}$.
nodes.statement_short: Optimal choice $R\approx x^{(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta)}$, $M\approx N\approx x/R$, $L\approx R^2/x$.

nodes.name: Barrier at $x^{2/3}$ and the case $M=N$
nodes.statement: Although our (conditional) results hit a barrier at $R = x^{5/8-o(1)}$, a more essential limitation of triple convolution estimates proven via the dispersion method lies at $R \le x^{2/3 - o(1)}$, corresponding to the case of three equal parameters $M = N = L \asymp x^{1/3}$. We note again that \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} allows for the case of two equal parameters $M = N \approx x/R$, for any $x^{1/2-o(1)} \ll R \ll x^{(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta)-o(1)}$; this is possible due to Maynard's deamplification argument \cite{maynard2020primes}. In particular, the ranges $M = N = x^{2/5}$, $L = x^{1/5}$, which were a limiting case in Drappeau's work \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 3]{drappeau2015theoremes}), are now admissible (this is analogous to the infamous case of convolving five sequences of equal sizes).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4 assuming Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be sufficiently small, let $C$ be the maximum between $\varepsilon^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}$ and the constant $C$ given by \cref{lem:harper}, and let $(\log x)^C \le y \le x^{1/C}$, $D := x^\varepsilon$, $\theta := \theta_{\max}$. Up to a scaling of $\varepsilon$, we want to show that \cref{eq:exponent} holds for the range of moduli \[ r \le x^{\alpha}, \qquad\qquad {\alpha} := \frac{5-4\theta}{8-6\theta} - 1000 \varepsilon, \] and we note that error terms of the form $O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\delta})$ are acceptable in \cref{eq:exponent} (up to slightly modifying the value of $\delta$), due to the inequality $x^{1-\delta} \ll \Psi(x, y) y^{-\delta/2}$ (see \cite[p.\ 856]{drappeau2015theoremes}). We may of course assume that $a_1$ and $a_2$ are relatively prime, by reducing any common factors. We split the left-hand side of \cref{eq:exponent} into \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{n\overline{a_1}a_2 \equiv 1 \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(n,r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} \right) \bigg\vert \\ &\le \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert + \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(n,r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ prim.},\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le D}} \chi(n\overline{a_1}a_2) \bigg\vert. \end{aligned} \] The second sum is just \[ \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{r} \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le D}} \chi(n) \bigg\vert , \] which is appropriately bounded by \cref{lem:harper} and the triangle inequality. It remains to bound the first sum. Note that the range $n \in S(x, y)$ means $n \le x$ and $P^+(n) \le y$, where $P^+(n)$ denotes the greatest prime factor of $n$. We bound the contribution of $n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon}$ trivially, as in \cite[p.\ 855]{drappeau2015theoremes}: \[ \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon} \\ P^+(n) \le y}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert \ll_\varepsilon x^{\alpha} + \sum_{\substack{n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon} \\ a_2 n \neq a_1}} \tau(|a_2n - a_1|) + x^{\varepsilon/2} \sum_{n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon}} 1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{1-\varepsilon/2}, \] and put the other $n$'s into $O(\log x)$ dyadic ranges $n \sim X$, with $x^{1-\varepsilon} \le X \ll x$. We also extend the range of $r$ in these sums to $r \le X^{{\alpha} + 10\varepsilon}$, noting that $x^{\alpha} \le x^{(1-\varepsilon)({\alpha} + 10\varepsilon)}$. Putting $r$ into $O(\log x)$ dyadic ranges $r \sim R$, it remains to bound sums of the form \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{n \sim X \\ P^+(n) \le y}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert, \end{equation} for $R \ll X^{{\alpha}+10\varepsilon}$. The contribution of the Bombieri--Vinogradov range $R \ll X^{(1/2) - (\varepsilon/10)}$ is handled by classical methods (e.g., using \cite[Theorem 17.4]{iwaniec2021analytic}; see \cite{drappeau2015theoremes,drappeau2017smooth}). For any $R$ in the remaining range $X^{(1/2) - (\varepsilon/10)} \le R \ll X^{{\alpha}+10\varepsilon}$, we set \begin{equation} M_0 := \frac{X^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad N_0 := \frac{X^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad L_0 := \frac{R^2}{X^{1-20\varepsilon}}, \end{equation} and factorize smooth numbers as in \cite[Lemme 7]{drappeau2015theoremes} to rewrite the sum in \cref{eq:sum-r-to-estimate} as \[ \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{L_0 < \ell \le L_0 P^-(\ell) \\ P^+(\ell) \le y}} \sum_{\substack{M_0 < m \le M_0 P^-(m) \\ P^+(m) \le P^-(\ell)}} \sum_{\substack{mn\ell \sim X \\ P^+(n) \le P^-(m)}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert, \] where $P^-(n)$ denotes the smallest prime factor of $n$. We also put $m, n, \ell$ into $O((\log y)^3)$ dyadic ranges $m \sim M$, $n \sim N$, $\ell \sim L$, with $M \in [M_0, yM_0]$, $N \in [y^{-2}N_0, N_0]$, $L \in [L_0, yL_0]$, and $MNL \asymp X$. Recalling that $y \le x^{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)} \le X^\varepsilon$, it is easily checked that for such $M, N, L$ and $X^{(1/2)-(\varepsilon/10)} \le R \ll X^{{\alpha}+10\varepsilon} = X^{(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta) - 990\varepsilon}$, and small enough $\varepsilon$, the conditions in \cref{eq:conditions} are satisfied (with respect to $X$ instead of $x$). At this point, our sums are almost in the right form to apply the triple convolution estimate in \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}, except for a few joint constraints on the variables $m, n, \ell$ (these are $P^+(m) \le P^-(\ell)$, $P^+(n) \le P^-(m)$, respectively $mn\ell \sim X$). The last step of analytically separating these constraints is identical to that in \cite[pp.\ 853--854]{drappeau2015theoremes}, except that in the end we apply \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} instead of \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 3]{drappeau2015theoremes}. Overall, the contribution of the range $X^{(1/2)-(\varepsilon/10)} \le R \ll X^{{\alpha} + 10\varepsilon}$ is $O_\varepsilon\left( (\log x)^{O(1)} x^{1-\delta} \right)$, which is acceptable; this completes our proof.
nodes.statement_short: Remove small-conductor characters via Harper's lemma, discard small $n$, then factor smooth numbers into dyadic triple convolutions and apply Theorem 4.1.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 1.5
nodes.statement: We only briefly note that the result for smooth-supported multiplicative functions in \cref{thm:distribution-functions} follows by an analogous modification to the arguments in \cite{drappeau2017smooth}, using the parameters in \cref{eq:parameters-2}, and \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} instead of \cite[Lemma 2.3]{drappeau2017smooth}. The main additional difficulty in \cite{drappeau2017smooth} lies in the contribution of the small-conductor characters, since \cref{lem:harper} is no longer applicable; as a replacement, Drappeau, Granville and Shao developed a large sieve inequality for smooth-supported sequences \cite[Theorem 5.1]{drappeau2017smooth}. (We also point the reader to the follow-up work of Shparlinski in \cite{shparlinski2018character}.)
nodes.statement_short: Modify Drappeau–Granville–Shao's argument using Theorem 4.1 and the parameters (4.6).

nodes.name: Combined sequence $u_k$
nodes.statement: We first combine the sequences $\beta_n$ and $\gamma_\ell$ into one sequence \begin{equation} u_k := \sum_{n\ell = k} \beta_n \gamma_\ell, \end{equation} supported in $(K, 4K]$ where $K := NL$, $|u_k| \le \tau(k) \ll_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2}$, and $\sum_k |u_k| \ll K$.
nodes.statement_short: $u_k=\sum_{n\ell=k}\beta_n\gamma_\ell$, supported in $(K,4K]$ with $K=NL$.

nodes.name: Dispersion quantity $\Delta$
nodes.statement: Denoting the left-hand side of \cref{eq:triple-conv-estimate} by $\Delta = \Delta_D(M,N,L,R)$, we can introduce coefficients $\rho_r$ of absolute value $1$, supported in $(R, 2R]$, to rewrite \[ \Delta = \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m, r) = 1} \alpha_m \sum_{(k, r) = 1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r) \right), \] where we recall that $\omega_D$ was defined in \cref{eq:omega-d}.
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta$ is the left side of (4.3), rewritten with unimodular weights $\rho_r$.

nodes.name: Deamplification parameter range for E
nodes.statement: For now, we require that \begin{equation} x^{4\varepsilon} \le E \ll x^{-\varepsilon} \frac{K}{R}, \end{equation} which is compatible with \cref{eq:conditions} since $R \ll x^{-5\varepsilon} NL$.
nodes.statement_short: The deamplification parameter satisfies $x^{4\varepsilon}\le E\ll x^{-\varepsilon}K/R$.

nodes.name: Averaging set of primes $\mathscr{E}$
nodes.statement: For multiple reasons of convenience throughout our proof, we will actually average over the set \begin{equation} \mathscr{E} := \{e \sim E : e \text{ prime},\ e \nmid a_2\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dispersion setup with deamplification
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi$ be a smooth function satisfying \begin{equation} \mathbbm{1}_{[1, 2]} \le \Phi \le \mathbbm{1}_{(0.5, 3)}, \end{equation} and $||\Phi^{(j)}||_\infty \ll_j 1$ for $j \ge 0$. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and $1 \gg \delta > 0$, under the parameter conditions in \cref{eq:conditions,eq:E-conditions}, one has \begin{equation} \Delta \ll_\varepsilon x\sqrt{\frac{R \log x}{K^2} (\mathcal{S}_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} \mathcal{S}_2 + \mathcal{S}_3)} + x^{1-\varepsilon}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_1 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re} \\ k_i \equiv a_1\overline{a_2m} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_2 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{(m,r)=1}} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_2 \equiv a_1\overline{a_2m} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \omega_D(mk_1 \overline{a_1}a_2; r)\overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_3 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{ (r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy–Schwarz with deamplification bounds $\Delta$ by the dispersion sums $\mathcal S_1-2\mathrm{Re}\mathcal S_2+\mathcal S_3$.
assumptions: Let $\Phi$ be a smooth function satisfying
nodes.label: prop:setup

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement: For a fixed prime $e \sim E$, we wish to eliminate the contribution to $\Delta$ of the terms $k$ with $(e, k) \neq 1$, i.e., $e \mid k$. This contribution is \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m, r) = 1} \alpha_m \sum_{\substack{e \mid k \in (K, 4K] \\ (k, r) = 1}} u_{k} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r) \right) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2e)=1}} \sum_{e \mid s \in (MK, 8MK]} x^{\varepsilon/2} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{s \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} + \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} D^2 \right) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon} \sum_{r \sim R} \left(\frac{MK}{RE} + 1 + \left(\frac{MK}{E} + 1\right) \frac{D^2}{R}\right) \quad \ll x^{\varepsilon} \left(\frac{xD^2}{E} + R + D^2\right) \ll x^{\varepsilon} \left(\frac{x^{1+2\varepsilon}}{x^{4\varepsilon}} + R + x^{2\varepsilon}\right), \end{aligned} \] which is $\ll x^{1-\varepsilon}$ since $R \ll x^{(2/3)-11\varepsilon}$ by \cref{eq:conditions}. It follows that \[ \Delta = \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m,r)=1} \alpha_m \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r) \right) + O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\varepsilon}), \] where we also made explicit the restriction $(mk, r) = 1$, required for the summand to be nonzero. Now for fixed $m$ and $e$ we have \[ \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} = \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}}, \] and there are precisely $\varphi(re)/\varphi(r)$ choices of $b$ in the summation; thus \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta &= \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m,r)=1} \alpha_m \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right) \\ &+ O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\varepsilon}). \end{aligned} \] (For a complete deamplification setup, one could also try to split the term $\omega_D(mk\overline{a_1}a_2; r)$ according to the residue $b$ of $k \pmod{re}$, but we do not need to do this in our proof.) We then average over $e$ in the set $\mathcal{E}$ from \cref{eq:averaging-set}, which has size $|\mathscr{E}| \asymp_\varepsilon E/\log E$ (recalling that $E \gg x^{\varepsilon}$ and $|a_2| \le x^\delta$). Thus up to an error of $O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\varepsilon})$, we can rewrite $\Delta$ as \[ \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m,r)=1} \alpha_m \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right). \] We now apply Cauchy--Schwarz in the $e,r,m,b$ variables, allowing us to eliminate the $\rho_r$ and $\alpha_m$ coefficients; this gives \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} |\Delta|^2 &\ll \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|^2} \left( \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \sum_{(m,r)=1} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} |\rho_r|^2 |\alpha_m|^2 \right) \Delta' + O_\varepsilon(x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}) \\ &\ll \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|^2} \left( \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2)=1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ (m,r)=1}} \frac{\varphi(re)}{\varphi(r)} \right) \Delta' + O_\varepsilon(x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon MR (\log E) \Delta' + x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where we used that $\varphi(re) \le \varphi(r) e$, and we denoted \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta' &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2)=1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ (m,r)=1}} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \] Anticipating a later application of Poisson summation, we bound the indicator functions $\mathbbm{1}_{m \sim M}$ and $\mathbbm{1}_{r \sim R}$ from above by $\Phi(m/M)$ and $\Phi(r/R)$. Then we expand the square and perform the $b$-summation to obtain \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \Delta' &\le \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{(r,a_1a_2)=1}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{(m,r)=1}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b\ (re)} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= M \left(\mathcal{S}_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} \mathcal{S}_2 + \mathcal{S}_3\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Combining \cref{eq:delta-squared} with \cref{eq:delta-prime} and recalling that $M \asymp x/K$, we recover \cref{eq:setup}.
nodes.statement_short: Discard $k$ divisible by $e$, split by residue mod $re$, average over primes $e\in\mathscr E$, then Cauchy–Schwarz in $e,r,m,b$ and expand the square.

nodes.name: Poisson difference $\mathcal{E}_r(c)$ and main terms $X_j$
nodes.statement: Thus if we define \begin{equation} \mathcal{E}_r(c) := \left(\frac{1}{M} \sum_{m \equiv c \pmod{r}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \right) - \frac{\widehat{\Phi}(0)}{r}, \end{equation} which can be estimated via the truncated Poisson summation in \cref{lem:poisson}, we can rewrite \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_1 &= \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_1 + \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re} \\ k_i \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_2 &= \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_2 + \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_2 \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \omega_D(k_1 \overline{a_1}a_2c; r)\overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_3 &= \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_3 + \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \omega_D(k \overline{a_1}a_2c; r)\right\vert^2, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} X_1 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ X_2 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \omega_D(k_1 \overline{k_2}; r), \\ X_3 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \omega_D(kc; r)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal E_r(c)$ is the deviation of the smoothed count of $m\equiv c$ (mod $r$) from $\hat\Phi(0)/r$; $X_j$ are the resulting main terms of $\mathcal S_j$.

nodes.name: Contribution of main terms
nodes.statement: With the notation above, one has \[ 0 \le X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 \ll \frac{K^2}{RD} (\log x)^6, \] under the parameter conditions in \cref{eq:conditions,eq:E-conditions}.
nodes.statement_short: The combined main term $X_1-2\mathrm{Re}X_2+X_3$ is $\ll K^2(\log x)^6/(RD)$.
nodes.label: prop:main-terms

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.1
nodes.statement: In analogy with \cref{eq:delta-prime}, we can write \[ \begin{aligned} &X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r, a_1a_2) = 1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv c \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(k\overline{c}; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &\ll \frac{1}{R} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{r} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(k\overline{b}; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{R} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_r \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)^2} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) \right)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \] Note that \[ \begin{aligned} \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) &= \left( \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; r) \right) + \left( \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; r) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) \right) \\ &= \sum_{\substack{\chi \in S}} \chi(k)\overline{\chi(b)}, \end{aligned} \] where $S = S(r,e,\varepsilon) = S_1 \cup S_2$ and \[ \begin{aligned} S_1 &:= \left\{ \chi \text{ primitive} : \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \nmid r, \text{ but } \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid re \right\}, \\ S_2 &:= \left\{ \chi \text{ primitive} : \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D \text{ and } \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r \right\}. \end{aligned} \] Since all the characters in $S$ are primitive, any distinct $\chi_1, \chi_2 \in S$ must induce different characters modulo $re$. Thus $\chi_1 \overline{\chi_2} \mathbbm{1}_{(re, \cdot) = 1}$ is not the principal character modulo $re$, so it must have average $0$. But then \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{\chi \in S} \overline{\chi}(b) \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k) \right\vert^2 \\ &= \sum_{\chi_1,\chi_2 \in S} \left(\sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi_1(k)\right)\overline{\left(\sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi_2(k)\right)} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \overline{\chi_1}(b) \chi_2(b) \\ &= \varphi(re) \sum_{\chi \in S} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \] We conclude that \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 \ &\ll \frac{1}{R}\sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_r \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{\chi \in S} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2 \\ &\le \frac{1}{R}\sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_r \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid re}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2, \end{aligned} \] where we used that all characters $\chi \in S_1$ also have $\textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D$, since $D \le x^\varepsilon < E \le e \mid \textnormal{cond}(\chi)$. Now letting $Q := RE$, substituting $q$ for $re$, and using that $q$ has $O(\log q)$ different prime factors, we can bound the sum above by \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 &\ll \frac{\log x}{R}\sum_{Q/2 \le q \le 6Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid q}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,q)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2. \\ &\le \frac{\log x}{R} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}}\, \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ s \mid q}} \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \left\vert \sum_{(k,q/s)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2 \\ &\le \frac{\log x}{R} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}}\, \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ s \mid q}} \frac{\tau(q/s)}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{d \mid q/s} \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(dk')\right\vert^2 \\ &\le \frac{\log x}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}}\, \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(k')\right\vert^2 \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ ds \mid q}} \frac{\tau(q/s)}{\varphi(q)}, \end{aligned} \] where we decomposed $\mathbbm{1}_{(a, b) = 1} = \sum_{d \mid (a, b)} \mu(d)$ to get rid of the coprimality restriction. Noting that \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ sd \mid q}} \frac{\tau(q/s)}{\varphi(q)} \le \sum_{\substack{q' \le 6Q}} \frac{\tau(q'd)}{\varphi(q'ds)} \le \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)\varphi(s)} \sum_{\substack{q' \le 6Q}} \frac{\tau(q')}{\varphi(q')} \ll \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)\varphi(s)} (\log x)^2, \] we further have \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 &\ll \frac{(\log x)^3}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(s)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}} \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(k')\right\vert^2 \\ &= \frac{(\log x)^3}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)} \int_D^\infty \sum_{D < s \le \min(6Q, t)} \frac{s}{\varphi(s)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}} \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(k')\right\vert^2 \frac{dt}{t^2}. \end{aligned} \] Finally, applying the multiplicative large sieve from \cref{lem:large-sieve} as in \cite[p.\ 900]{drappeau2017smooth} (see also the top of \cite[p.\ 852]{drappeau2015theoremes}, which misses a factor of $(\tau(d) \log K)^2$), we conclude that \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2 \textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 &\ll \frac{(\log x)^2}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)}{d\varphi(d)} \int_D^\infty \left(\frac{K}{d} + \min(6Q, t)^2 \right) \sum_{k' \asymp K/d} |u_{dk'}|^2\ \frac{dt}{t^2} \\ &\ll \frac{(\log x)^3}{R} K (\log K)^3 \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)^3}{d\varphi(d)} \left( \frac{K}{dD} + Q \right) \\ &\ll (\log x)^6 \frac{K}{R} \left(\frac{K}{D} + Q\right) \\ &\ll (\log x)^6 K^2 (RD)^{-1}, \end{aligned} \] as we wanted. In the last line, we made use of the condition $RE \ll x^{-\varepsilon}K$ (from \cref{eq:E-conditions}) to bound $Q = RE \ll K/D$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the main terms as a square, use character orthogonality to reduce to characters of conductor $>D$, then apply the multiplicative large sieve.

nodes.name: Estimates for dispersion sums
nodes.statement: For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that with the notation in \cref{eq:sums-2}, the following hold: \begin{itemize} \item[(i).] Assuming the ranges in \cref{eq:conditions}, there exists a choice of $E$ satisfying \cref{eq:E-conditions} such that \begin{equation} \mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}. \end{equation} \item[(ii).] Assuming both \cref{eq:conditions,eq:E-conditions}, one has \begin{align} \mathcal{S}_2 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_2 &\ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}, \\ \mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_3 &\ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}. \end{align} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Each dispersion sum $\mathcal S_j$ is within $x^{-2\delta}K^2/R$ of its main term $\hat\Phi(0)X_j$.
conclusions: there exists a choice of $E$ satisfying \cref{eq:E-conditions} such that \begin{equation} \mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}. \end{equation}
there exists a choice of $E$ satisfying \cref{eq:E-conditions} such that \begin{equation} \mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}. \end{equation}

nodes.label: prop:dispersion-sums

nodes.name: Proposition 6.2(i): estimate for $\mathcal{S}_1$
nodes.statement: Assuming the ranges in \cref{eq:conditions}, there exists a choice of $E$ satisfying \cref{eq:E-conditions} such that \begin{equation} \mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}. \end{equation}
conclusions: there exists a choice of $E$ satisfying \cref{eq:E-conditions} such that \begin{equation} \mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}.

nodes.name: Estimate (6.5) for $\mathcal{S}_2$
nodes.statement: \mathcal{S}_2 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_2 &\ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R},
nodes.label: eq:S2-estimate

nodes.name: Estimate (6.6) for $\mathcal{S}_3$
nodes.statement: \mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_3 &\ll_\varepsilon x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}.
nodes.label: eq:S3-estimate

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1 assuming Proposition 6.2
nodes.statement: The hypothesis of \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} assumes \cref{eq:conditions}, so we can pick $E$ as in \cref{prop:dispersion-sums}.$(i)$, subject to \cref{eq:E-conditions}. Then, by combining \cref{prop:setup,prop:dispersion-sums,prop:main-terms}, we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta &\ll_\varepsilon x\sqrt{\frac{R\log x}{K^2} \left(\widehat{\Phi}(0)\frac{K^2}{RD}(\log x)^6 + x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R} \right)} + x^{1-\varepsilon} \\ &\ll x\sqrt{(\log x)^7 \left(\frac{1}{D} + \frac{1}{x^{2\delta}}\right)} + x^{1-\varepsilon} \end{aligned} \] The conclusion of \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} follows after replacing $\delta$ with $\min(\delta, \varepsilon)$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Propositions 5.1, 6.1 and 6.2 and simplify.

nodes.name: Proof of (6.6), estimating $\mathcal{S}_3$
nodes.statement: Recall from \cref{eq:sums-2} that \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_3 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \sum_{\substack{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k \overline{a_1}a_2 c)\right\vert^2 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{\chi_1, \chi_2 \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi_i) \mid r}} \overline{\chi_1} \chi_2 (a_1 \overline{a_2}) \sum_{\substack{k_1, k_2 \\ (k_1k_2, re) = 1}} \chi_1(k_1) u_{k_1} \overline{\chi_2(k_2) u_{k_2}} \\ & \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad \times \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c) \mathcal{E}_r(c), \end{aligned} \] where $\mathcal{E}_r(c)$ is given by \cref{eq:Poisson-difference}. Expanding $\mathcal{E}_r(c)$ according to \cref{lem:poisson} with $H := x^\varepsilon R M^{-1}$, we obtain \begin{equation} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c) \mathcal{E}_r(c) = \frac{1}{r} \sum_{0 < |h| < H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c)\ \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{ch}{r}\right) + O_\varepsilon\left(x^{-100}\right). \end{equation} (In such manipulations, we warn the reader of the potential confusion between the integer variable $e \in \mathscr{E}$ and the function $\textnormal{e}(\cdot)$; the difference should be clear from context.) The inner sum (over $c$) in \cref{eq:Gauss} is a Gauss sum, which we can bound using \cref{lem:gauss} for the Dirichlet character $\chi_1 \overline{\chi_2} \mathbbm{1}_{(\cdot, r) = 1} \pmod{r}$ (whose conductor divides $r$ and is at most equal to $D^2 \le x^{2\varepsilon}$). This yields \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c) \mathcal{E}_r(c) &\ll_\varepsilon x^{-100} + \frac{1}{r} \sum_{0 < |h| < H} x^\varepsilon \sum_{d \mid (h, r)} d \\ &\ll x^{-100} + \frac{x^\varepsilon}{r} \sum_{d \mid r} d \sum_{0 < |h| < H/d} 1 \ll \frac{x^{\varepsilon}}{R} \tau(r) H = x^{2\varepsilon} \frac{\tau(r)}{M}, \end{aligned} \] which leads to \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_3 \ll_\varepsilon x^{2\varepsilon} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{\tau(r)}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re) M} |\mathcal{X}_D|^2 K^2 &\ll x^{6\varepsilon} \frac{K^2}{M} \sum_{r} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{\tau(r)}{\varphi(r)^2} \\ &\ll x^{6\varepsilon} \frac{K^2}{MR} (\log R)^{O(1)}, \end{aligned} \] using that $\varphi(re) \gg \varphi(r) e$ (since $e$ is prime). Since $x/M \asymp K \ll x^{(2/3)-6\varepsilon}$ by \cref{eq:conditions}, we have $M \gg x^{1/3+6\varepsilon} \gg x^{7\varepsilon}$ for small enough $\varepsilon$, and in particular $\mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_3\ll_\varepsilon x^{-\varepsilon} K^2/R$, proving the easier third of \cref{prop:dispersion-sums}.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\mathcal E_r(c)$ by truncated Poisson; the $c$-sums are Gauss sums bounded by Lemma 3.6.

nodes.name: Proof of (6.5), estimating $\mathcal{S}_2$
nodes.statement: Recall from \cref{eq:sums-2} that \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{S}_2 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_2 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_2 \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \sum_{\substack{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k_1 \overline{a_1} a_2 c) \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D} \sum_{(k_1 k_2, e) = 1} \chi(k_1) u_{k_1} \overline{\chi(k_2) u_{k_2}} \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \mathcal{E}_r(a_1 \overline{a_2 k_2}). \end{aligned} \] Applying \cref{lem:poisson} with $H := x^\varepsilon R M^{-1}$ to expand $\mathcal{E}_r(a_1\overline{a_2 k_2})$ (as given in \cref{eq:Poisson-difference}), we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{S}_2 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_2 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D} \sum_{(k_1 k_2, e) = 1} \chi(k_1) u_{k_1} \overline{\chi(k_2) u_{k_2}} \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \frac{1}{r\varphi(re)} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{a_1 h \overline{a_2k_2}}{r}\right) \\ &+ O_\varepsilon\left(x^{-90}\right), \end{aligned} \] where we used that $\varphi(re) \gg \varphi(r) e$ as before (since $e$ is prime). The error term is acceptable, so let us focus on the main term in the right-hand side (denote this by $Y_2$). By \cref{lem:bezout}, we have \[ \frac{\overline{a_2 k_2}}{r} + \frac{\overline{r}}{a_2 k_2} \equiv \frac{1}{a_2 k_2 r} \quad \pmod{1}, \] so that \begin{equation} Y_2 \ll \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D} \sum_{k_1, k_2} |u_{k_1} u_{k_2}| \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \frac{1}{r\varphi(re)} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{a_1 h}{a_2 k_2 r} - \frac{a_1 h\overline{r}}{a_2 k_2}\right) \right\vert. \end{equation} At this point we decompose \[ \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} = \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \left(\frac{1}{e-1} - \frac{1}{e(e-1)} \mathbbm{1}_{e \mid r} \right), \] aiming to apply the exponential sum bound in \cref{lem:incomplete-weil}. Fixing $e, a_i, k_i, h$, this lets us rewrite the sum over $r$ in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:Y2} as \[ \frac{1}{e-1} Z_2(\textnormal{cond}(\chi)) - \frac{1}{e(e-1)} Z_2([\textnormal{cond}(\chi), e]), \] where \[ Z_2(\ell) := \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \ell \mid r}} u(r) \frac{r}{\varphi(r)}\ \textnormal{e} \left(-\frac{a_1 h\overline{r}}{a_2k_2} \right) \] and \[ u(r) := \frac{1}{r^2} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e} \left( \frac{a_1h}{a_2k_2 r} \right). \] Note that $u$ extends to a differentiable function of a real variable $\xi$, supported in $[R/2, 3R/2]$, and with derivative bounds \[ \begin{aligned} |u'(\xi)| &\ll \frac{1}{R^3} + \frac{1}{R^2} \left(\frac{1}{R} + \frac{HM}{R^2} + \frac{|a_1| H}{KR^2} \right) \\ &\ll \frac{1}{R^2} \left(\frac{1}{R} + \frac{x^\varepsilon R}{R^2} + \frac{|a_1| x^\varepsilon R}{xR^2} \right) \quad \ll \frac{x^{2\varepsilon}}{R^3}. \end{aligned} \] in this region (we used that $H = x^\varepsilon R M^{-1}$, $MK \asymp x$, and the very crude bound $|a_1| \ll x^{1+\varepsilon}$).
