Then given a 5-variable smooth function $g(t_1, \ldots, t_5)$ with compact support in $t_1 \asymp 1$, and bounded derivatives $||\frac{\partial^{\sum j_i}}{\prod (\partial t_i)^{j_i}} g||_\infty \ll_{j_1,\ldots,j_5} 1$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ n \sim N}} \textnormal{e}(m\omega)\, b_{n,r,s} &\sum_{(c, r) = 1} g\left(\frac{c}{C}, \frac{m}{M}, \frac{n}{N}, \frac{r}{R}, \frac{s}{S}\right)\, S(m\overline{r}, \pm n; sc) \\ \ll_\varepsilon (CMNRS)^\varepsilon &\left(1 + \frac{CS\sqrt{R}}{\max(M, RS) \sqrt{\max(N, RS)}} \right)^{\theta_{\max}} \sqrt{MRS}\, ||b_{n,r,s}||_2\, \\ &\times \frac{\left(CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN} + C\sqrt{SM}\right)\left(CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN} + C\sqrt{SN}\right)}{CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Multilinear bound for sums of Kloosterman sums $S(m\bar r,\pm n;sc)$ with explicit dependence on $\theta_{\max}$.
assumptions: Let $C, M, N, R, S \gg 1$, $(b_{n,r,s})$ be a complex sequence, and $\omega \in \mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$

given a 5-variable smooth function $g(t_1, \ldots, t_5)$ with compact support in $t_1 \asymp 1$, and bounded derivatives $||\frac{\partial^{\sum j_i}}{\prod (\partial t_i)^{j_i}} g||_\infty \ll_{j_1,\ldots,j_5} 1$
conclusions: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ n \sim N}} \textnormal{e}(m\omega)\, b_{n,r,s} &\sum_{(c, r) = 1} g\left(\frac{c}{C}, \frac{m}{M}, \frac{n}{N}, \frac{r}{R}, \frac{s}{S}\right)\, S(m\overline{r}, \pm n; sc) \\ \ll_\varepsilon (CMNRS)^\varepsilon &\left(1 + \frac{CS\sqrt{R}}{\max(M, RS) \sqrt{\max(N, RS)}} \right)^{\theta_{\max}} \sqrt{MRS}\, ||b_{n,r,s}||_2\, \\ &\times \frac{\left(CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN} + C\sqrt{SM}\right)\left(CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN} + C\sqrt{SN}\right)}{CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN}}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.label: thm:di-kloosterman

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10.2
nodes.statement: We follow the proof of \cite[Theorem 11]{deshouillers1982kloosterman} in \cite[Section 9.1]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, reducing to the case of smooth functions of the form $\frac{CS\sqrt{R}}{cs\sqrt{r}} f \left(\frac{4\pi \sqrt{mn}}{cs\sqrt{r}}\right)$ (up to using slightly different values of $\omega$ and $b_{n,r,s}$); here $f(t)$ is a smooth function supported in $t \asymp X^{-1}$, for $X := CS\sqrt{R}/\sqrt{MN}$. After applying the Kuznetsov formula, we bound the contribution of the exceptional spectrum more carefully; as in \cite[p.\ 279]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, this is given by \[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{exc}} := CS\sqrt{R} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{j \ge 1 \\ \lambda_{j,rs} < 1/4}} \frac{\widehat{f}(\kappa_{j,rs})}{\textnormal{ch}(\pi \kappa_{j,rs})} \left( \sum_{m \sim M} \textnormal{e}(m\omega)\, \overline{\rho_{j,\infty}}(m) \right) \left( \sum_{n \sim N} b'_{n,r,s}\, \rho_{j,1/s}(n) \right), \] where \[ b'_{n,r,s} := \textnormal{e}\left(-n \frac{\overline{s}}{r}\right) b_{n,r,s}. \] Using the bounds $\textnormal{ch}(\pi \kappa_{j,rs}) \asymp 1$ and \[ |\widehat{f}(\kappa_{j,rs})| \ll \frac{1 + X^{2|\kappa_{j,rs}|}}{1 + X^{-1}} \ll (1 + X)^{\theta_{j,rs}} \] (see \cite[(7.1)]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}), and denoting \[ X_0 := \frac{1 + X}{\sqrt{X_1 X_2}} \le 1 + \frac{X}{\sqrt{X_1 X_2}}, \] for some $X_1, X_2 \ge 1$ to be chosen shortly, we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_{\text{exc}} \ll CS\sqrt{R} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{j \ge 1 \\ \lambda_{j,rs} < 1/4}} \left(X_0 \sqrt{X_1 X_2}\right)^{\theta_{j,rs}} \left\vert \sum_{m \sim M} \overline{\textnormal{e}(m\omega)}\, \rho_{j,\infty}(m) \right\vert \left\vert \sum_{n \sim N} b'_{n,r,s}\, \rho_{j,1/s}(n) \right\vert \\ \ll CS\sqrt{R}\ \frac{\left(1 + X_0\right)^{\theta_{\max}}}{1 + X^{-1}} \left(\sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S}} \sum_{\substack{j \ge 1 \\ \lambda_{j,rs} < 1/4}} X_1^{\theta_{j,rs}} \left\vert \sum_{m \sim M} \textnormal{e}(-m\omega)\, \rho_{j,\infty}(m) \right\vert^2 \right)^{1/2} \\ \times \left(\sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ s \sim S \\ (r, s) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{j \ge 1 \\ \lambda_{j,rs} < 1/4}} X_2^{\theta_{j,rs}} \left\vert \sum_{n \sim N} b'_{n,r,s}\, \rho_{j,1/s}(n) \right\vert^2 \right)^{1/2}, \end{aligned} \] by Cauchy--Schwarz. Recall that $\mu(1/s) = \mu(\infty) = (rs)^{-1}$ since $(r, s) = 1$; thus using the divisor bound and \cref{lem:di-large-sieve}, we conclude that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_{\text{exc}} \ll_\varepsilon (MNRS)^\varepsilon\, CS\sqrt{R}\, \frac{\left(1 + X_0\right)^{\theta_{\max}}}{1 + X^{-1}} \sqrt{RS} \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{M}{RS}}\right) \sqrt{M} \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{RS}}\right) ||b_{n,r,s}||_2 \\ \ll (MNRS)^\varepsilon \left(1 + \frac{CS\sqrt{R}}{\sqrt{MNX_1X_2}}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} \sqrt{MRS}\, ||b_{n,r,s}||_2 \\ \times \frac{\left(CS\sqrt{R} + C\sqrt{SM}\right)\left(CS\sqrt{R} + C\sqrt{SN}\right)}{CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN}}, \end{aligned} \] for $X_1 = \max(M, R^2S^2M^{-1})$ (coming from \cref{eq:like-di-thm-7}), and $X_2 = \max(1, RSN^{-1})$ (from \cref{eq:like-di-thm-5}). Up to minor rearrangements, this completes our proof.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Deshouillers–Iwaniec's proof of Theorem 11 via Kuznetsov, bounding the exceptional spectrum by Cauchy–Schwarz and the large sieve inequalities of Lemma 10.1.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.9
nodes.statement: We swap the $m$ and $n$ variables, and pick the second term in each maximum from \cref{eq:like-di-thm-11} for an upper bound, resulting in a $\theta$-factor of \[ \left(1 + \frac{C}{R\sqrt{S}} \right)^{\theta_{\max}}. \] We also rewrite the last fraction in \cref{eq:like-di-thm-11} as \[ CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN} + C\sqrt{SM} + C\sqrt{SN} + \frac{C^2 S \sqrt{MN}}{CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN}}, \] and we use the lower bound $CS\sqrt{R} + \sqrt{MN} \ge CS\sqrt{R}$ in the final term. To reduce to a smooth function depending only on $c$, we can take \[ g(t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4, t_5) = g_1\left(t_1\right) g_2\left(t_2\right) g_3\left(t_3\right) g_4\left(t_4\right) g_5\left(t_5\right), \] for some smooth compactly supported functions $g_i$, where $g_2, g_3, g_4, g_5$ are equal to $1$ on $[1, 2]$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 10.2: swap $m,n$, take the larger terms in the maxima, and reduce to a smooth weight in $c$.

nodes.name: Equation (1.1): Bombieri–Vinogradov bound
nodes.statement: \sum_{q \le x^{1/2}/(\log x)^B} \sup_{(a, q) = 1} \left\vert \pi(x; q, a) - \frac{\pi(x)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A},
nodes.label: eq:bv

nodes.name: Equation (1.2): Exponent of distribution alpha
nodes.statement: \alpha := \frac{5-4\theta_{\max}}{8-6\theta_{\max}} - \varepsilon,
nodes.label: eq:exponent-theta

nodes.name: Equation (1.3): Smooth numbers equidistribution bound
nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{\alpha} \\ (q, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a_1 \overline{a_2}, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon, A} \Psi(x, y) \left(H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta}\right),
nodes.label: eq:exponent

nodes.name: Equation (2.1)
nodes.statement: \sum_{r \sim R} \rho_r \sum_{m \sim M} \alpha_m \sum_{n \sim N} \beta_n \sum_{\ell \sim L} \gamma_\ell \left(1_{mn\ell \equiv 1 \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(mn\ell, r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} \right) \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A},
nodes.label: eq:sketch-triple-conv

nodes.name: Equation (2.2)
nodes.statement: M := \frac{x^{1-\delta}}{R}, \qquad\qquad N := \frac{x^{1-2\delta}}{R}, \qquad\qquad L := \frac{R^2}{x^{1-3\delta}},
nodes.label: eq:sketch-ranges

nodes.name: Equation (2.3)
nodes.statement: \sum_{r \sim R}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N} \beta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \\ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{r}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} \textnormal{e}\left(h \frac{\overline{k}}{r} \right),
nodes.label: eq:sketch-main-exponential

nodes.name: Equation (2.4)
nodes.statement: \sum_{t \sim x^\delta}\, \sum_{\ell_1 \sim L}\, \sum_{h_2 \sim R/M} x^{o(1)} \sum_{k \sim NL} \sum_{\substack{n \sim N \\ n \equiv k\overline{\ell_1} \pmod{t}}} 1 \ll x^{o(1)} RNL^2 \frac{N}{M},
nodes.label: eq:sketch-diagonal-terms

nodes.name: Equation (2.5)
nodes.statement: \sum_{t \sim x^\delta} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ell_2 \sim L \\ \ell_1 \equiv \ell_2 \pmod{t} \\ \ell_1 \neq \ell_2}} \sum_{\substack{h_1, h_2 \sim R/M \\ h_1\ell_2 \neq h_2\ell_1}} \left\vert \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{j\overline{\ell_1}}{t}\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left((h_1\ell_2 - h_2\ell_1)\overline{\ell_1\ell_2}, j; k\right)\right\vert,
nodes.label: eq:sketch-final-sum

nodes.name: Equation (2.6)
nodes.statement: \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_d \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{j\overline{\ell_1}}{t}\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; k\right).
nodes.label: eq:sketch-kloosterman

nodes.name: Equation (2.8)
nodes.statement: 4\sigma < \frac{1}{10} - \frac{\theta_{\max}}{2}.
nodes.label: eq:sketch-sigma

nodes.name: Equation (2.9)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\ell_1,\ell_2 \sim L}\, \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_{d,\ell_1,\ell_2} \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(j\omega\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; k\right),
nodes.section: 2.2 Improved exponential sum manipulations for specific ranges
nodes.label: eq:sketch-kloosterman-2

nodes.name: Equation (4.1): Definition of omega_D
nodes.statement: \omega_D(k; r) := \sum_{\substack{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k), \qquad\quad \text{where} \qquad\quad \mathcal{X}_D := \{\chi \text{ primitive} : \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le D\},
nodes.label: eq:omega-d

nodes.name: Equation (4.2): Parameter conditions
nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} a_1, a_2 \ll x^\delta, \qquad MNL \asymp x, \qquad\quad x^{(1-\varepsilon)/2} \ll R \ll x^{-5\varepsilon} NL \ll x^{(2/3) - 11\varepsilon}, \qquad N^9 L^8 \ll x^3 R^4, \\ N \ll \frac{x^{1-2\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad N^4 L^7 \max(1, N/L)^{2\theta} \ll x^{2-16\varepsilon}R^2, \qquad N^{12-6\theta} L^{11-6\theta} \ll x^{6-4(\theta+\varepsilon)} R^2, \end{gathered}
nodes.label: eq:conditions

nodes.name: Equation (4.3): Triple convolution bound
nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \sum_{m \sim M} \sum_{n \sim N} \sum_{\ell \sim L} \alpha_m \beta_n \gamma_\ell\, \mathcal{E}_D(mn\ell \overline{a_1} a_2; r) \right\vert \ll_\varepsilon \frac{x (\log x)^4}{\min\left(x^\delta, \sqrt{D}\right)},
nodes.label: eq:triple-conv-estimate

nodes.name: Equation (4.4): Optimal parameters
nodes.statement: R \approx x^{(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta)}, \qquad\quad M \approx \frac{x}{R}, \qquad\quad N \approx \frac{x}{R}, \qquad\quad L \approx \frac{R^2}{x}.
nodes.label: eq:optimal-parameters

nodes.name: Equation (4.5)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{n \sim X \\ P^+(n) \le y}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert,
nodes.label: eq:sum-r-to-estimate

nodes.name: Equation (4.6)
nodes.statement: M_0 := \frac{X^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad N_0 := \frac{X^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad L_0 := \frac{R^2}{X^{1-20\varepsilon}},
nodes.label: eq:parameters-2

nodes.name: Equation (5.1): Definition of u_k
nodes.statement: u_k := \sum_{n\ell = k} \beta_n \gamma_\ell,
nodes.label: eq:u-def

nodes.name: Equation (5.2): Conditions on E
nodes.statement: x^{4\varepsilon} \le E \ll x^{-\varepsilon} \frac{K}{R},
nodes.label: eq:E-conditions

nodes.name: Equation (5.3): Averaging set of primes
nodes.statement: \mathscr{E} := \{e \sim E : e \text{ prime},\ e \nmid a_2\}.
nodes.label: eq:averaging-set

nodes.name: Equation (5.4)
nodes.statement: \mathbbm{1}_{[1, 2]} \le \Phi \le \mathbbm{1}_{(0.5, 3)},
nodes.label: eq:phi-smooth

nodes.name: Equation (5.5): Dispersion bound for Delta
nodes.statement: \Delta \ll_\varepsilon x\sqrt{\frac{R \log x}{K^2} (\mathcal{S}_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} \mathcal{S}_2 + \mathcal{S}_3)} + x^{1-\varepsilon},
nodes.label: eq:setup

nodes.name: Equation (5.6): Dispersion sums S_1, S_2, S_3
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_1 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re} \\ k_i \equiv a_1\overline{a_2m} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_2 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{(m,r)=1}} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_2 \equiv a_1\overline{a_2m} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \omega_D(mk_1 \overline{a_1}a_2; r)\overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_3 &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{ (r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:sums

nodes.name: Equation (5.7)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} |\Delta|^2 &\ll \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|^2} \left( \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \sum_{(m,r)=1} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} |\rho_r|^2 |\alpha_m|^2 \right) \Delta' + O_\varepsilon(x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}) \\ &\ll \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|^2} \left( \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2)=1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ (m,r)=1}} \frac{\varphi(re)}{\varphi(r)} \right) \Delta' + O_\varepsilon(x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon MR (\log E) \Delta' + x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}, \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:delta-squared

nodes.name: Equation (5.8)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \Delta' &\le \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{(r,a_1a_2)=1}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{(m,r)=1}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b\ (re)} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= M \left(\mathcal{S}_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} \mathcal{S}_2 + \mathcal{S}_3\right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:delta-prime

nodes.name: Equation (6.1): Poisson difference E_r(c)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{E}_r(c) := \left(\frac{1}{M} \sum_{m \equiv c \pmod{r}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \right) - \frac{\widehat{\Phi}(0)}{r},
nodes.label: eq:Poisson-difference

nodes.name: Equation (6.2): Dispersion sums minus main terms
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_1 &= \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_1 + \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re} \\ k_i \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_2 &= \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_2 + \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_2 \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \omega_D(k_1 \overline{a_1}a_2c; r)\overline{u_{k_2}}, \\ \mathcal{S}_3 &= \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_3 + \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \omega_D(k \overline{a_1}a_2c; r)\right\vert^2, \end{aligned}

nodes.name: Equation (6.3): Main terms X_j

nodes.name: Reduce to a triple convolution estimate
nodes.statement: Let us give a very rough sketch of our argument, for a simpler case of \cref{thm:distribution-simplified}. Consider the residue $a = 1$, the smoothness parameter $y = x^{1/\sqrt{\log \log x}}$, and a sum over moduli just above the $3/5$ threshold, say \[ r \le R := x^{3/5 + \sigma}, \] for some small $\sigma \gg 1$ (we switch the variable $q$ to $r$, following \cite{drappeau2015theoremes,drappeau2017smooth}). Using the factorization properties of smooth numbers, it suffices to prove a triple convolution estimate roughly of the form \begin{equation} \sum_{r \sim R} \rho_r \sum_{m \sim M} \alpha_m \sum_{n \sim N} \beta_n \sum_{\ell \sim L} \gamma_\ell \left(1_{mn\ell \equiv 1 \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(mn\ell, r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} \right) \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A}, \end{equation} where $(\rho_r)$, $(\alpha_m)$, $(\beta_n)$, $(\gamma_\ell)$ are arbitrary $1$-bounded complex sequences, but we are free to choose the parameters $M, N, L \gg 1$ subject to $MNL \asymp x$. We pick \begin{equation} M := \frac{x^{1-\delta}}{R}, \qquad\qquad N := \frac{x^{1-2\delta}}{R}, \qquad\qquad L := \frac{R^2}{x^{1-3\delta}}, \end{equation} for some small $\delta = o(1)$; thus $M, N \approx x^{2/5-\sigma}$ and $L \approx x^{1/5+2\sigma}$. Note additionally that $NL = x^{\delta} R$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the simplified case to a triple convolution estimate with chosen lengths $M,N,L$.

nodes.name: Limitations of the previous dispersion approach
nodes.statement: Following previous works \cite{bombieri1986primes,drappeau2015theoremes,maynard2020primes} based on the \emph{dispersion method}, we apply Cauchy--Schwarz in the $r, m$ variables, expand the square, and Fourier-complete the resulting sums in $m$ to sums over $h$. Ignoring GCD-constraints, the key resulting exponential sum is a smoothed variant of \begin{equation} \sum_{r \sim R}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N} \beta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \\ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{r}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} \textnormal{e}\left(h \frac{\overline{k}}{r} \right), \end{equation} where $(u_k)$ is the convolution of the original sequences $(\beta_n)$, $(\gamma_\ell)$. We flip moduli in the exponential via Bezout's identity, and substitute $t := (k - n\ell)/r$ to reduce to sums of the form \[ \sum_{t \sim x^\delta}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N} \beta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \\ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{t}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} \textnormal{e}\left(h t \frac{\overline{n\ell}}{k} \right). \] Following Maynard \cite{maynard2020primes}, we apply Cauchy--Schwarz in the $t, n, k$ variables (keeping the congruence modulo $t$ inside), and expand the square to reach the sum \[ \sum_{t \sim x^\delta} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ell_2 \sim L \\ \ell_1 \equiv \ell_2 \pmod{t}}} \gamma_{\ell_1} \overline{\gamma_{\ell_2}} \sum_{h_1, h_2 \sim R/M} \sum_{k \sim NL} \sum_{\substack{n \sim N \\ n \equiv k\overline{\ell_1} \pmod{t}}} \textnormal{e}\left(t(h_1 \ell_2 - h_2 \ell_1) \frac{\overline{n\ell_1\ell_2}}{k} \right), \] which we ultimately need to bound by $\ll_A RNL^2 (\log x)^{-A}$; note that the trivial bound is larger by about $(R/M)^2$, due to the sum over $h_1, h_2$ introduced by Poisson summation. We bound the contribution of the diagonal terms (with $h_1\ell_2 = h_2\ell_1$) by \begin{equation} \sum_{t \sim x^\delta}\, \sum_{\ell_1 \sim L}\, \sum_{h_2 \sim R/M} x^{o(1)} \sum_{k \sim NL} \sum_{\substack{n \sim N \\ n \equiv k\overline{\ell_1} \pmod{t}}} 1 \ll x^{o(1)} RNL^2 \frac{N}{M}, \end{equation} which is acceptable since $N/M = x^{-\delta}$. We then introduce Kloosterman sums $S(i, j; k)$ by completing the sum in $n$ to a sum over $j$, and find acceptable contributions from the zeroth Fourier coefficient ($j = 0$), as well as from the terms with $\ell_1 = \ell_2$; here it suffices to use the Weil bound, respectively an estimate of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite[Theorem 9]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}. It ultimately remains to bound a variant of \begin{equation} \sum_{t \sim x^\delta} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ell_2 \sim L \\ \ell_1 \equiv \ell_2 \pmod{t} \\ \ell_1 \neq \ell_2}} \sum_{\substack{h_1, h_2 \sim R/M \\ h_1\ell_2 \neq h_2\ell_1}} \left\vert \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{j\overline{\ell_1}}{t}\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left((h_1\ell_2 - h_2\ell_1)\overline{\ell_1\ell_2}, j; k\right)\right\vert, \end{equation} by $\ll_A N^2 L^4 (\log x)^{-A}$. Inserting $1$-bounded coefficients $\xi_{h_1, h_2}$ (also depending on $t, \ell_1, \ell_2, \omega$), and letting $a_d := \sum_{h_1 \ell_2 - h_2 \ell_1 = d} \xi_{h_1, h_2}$, the sum over $h_1, h_2$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} roughly reduces to \begin{equation} \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_d \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{j\overline{\ell_1}}{t}\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; k\right). \end{equation} Such sums can be bounded using the spectral theory of automorphic forms, specifically through the aforementioned work of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite{deshouillers1982kloosterman} (based on the Kuznetsov trace formula and the Weil bound); the relevant \emph{level} of the congruence group in \cref{not:exceptional} is $Q = \ell_1\ell_2$. Indeed, Maynard \cite{maynard2020primes} uses \cite[Theorem 9]{deshouillers1982kloosterman} to bound (a smoothed variant of) the sum in \cref{eq:sketch-kloosterman} by \[ x^{\theta_Q/2 + o(1)} NL^{5/2} \left(\sum_{d \sim RL/M} |a_d|^2\right)^{1/2}, \] and consequently the sum in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} by \begin{equation} x^{\theta_{\max}/2 + o(1)} NL^{5/2} \frac{R^{3/2}L^{3/2}}{M^{3/2}} \approx x^{(\theta_{\max}+3)/2 + 10\sigma}. \end{equation} Unfortunately, this falls short of the desired bound of $N^2 L^4 (\log x)^{-A} \approx x^{8/5 + 6\sigma}$, unless \begin{equation} 4\sigma < \frac{1}{10} - \frac{\theta_{\max}}{2}. \end{equation} This is (barely) impossible with the currently best-known bound of $\theta_{\max}/2 \le 7/64 \approx 0.109$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispersion, Poisson and Maynard's Cauchy–Schwarz lead to Kloosterman sums whose DI bound only reaches $x^{3/5}$ with current $\theta_{\max}$.

nodes.name: Level-averaged DI bound for specific ranges
nodes.statement: Starting from the work of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, better bounds (in the $\theta$-aspect) for sums like \cref{eq:sketch-kloosterman} have been available when one additionally averages over the level $\ell_1\ell_2$, and at least one of the sequences of coefficients is independent of the level. Indeed, Drappeau's triple convolution estimate \cite{drappeau2015theoremes} and prior works rely on \cite[Theorem 12]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, which gives such a result for incomplete Kloosterman sums. Following Maynard's argument (which is in turn based on Bombieri--Friedlander--Iwaniec's work in \cite[\S 10]{bombieri1987primes2}), we prefer to complete our Kloosterman sums, bound the contribution from the zeroth Fourier coefficient by hand, and separate into terms with $\ell_1 = \ell_2$ and $\ell_1 \neq \ell_2$, all before invoking Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds. We then aim to apply an optimized bound for sums of complete Kloosterman sums with averaging over the level (given in \cref{thm:di-type-bound}), which improves \cite[Theorem 11]{deshouillers1982kloosterman} by making the dependence on the $\theta_{\max}$ parameter explicit. But for this strategy to work out, we would need: \begin{itemize} \item[(1).] The range of $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} to be (discretely) dense inside $[L, 2L]^2$, and \item[(2).] Crucially, the coefficients $e\left(j \overline{\ell_1} / t \right)$ to not depend on $\ell_1, \ell_2$. \end{itemize} While (2) is obviously false in our case, it is only barely false for the specific ranges in \cref{eq:sketch-ranges}, due to the smallness of the parameter $t \sim x^\delta$. In particular, losing a factor of at most $x^{O(\delta)} = x^{o(1)}$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum}, we may fix $t$ and the values of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2 \pmod{t}$, turning (2) into a true statement at the expense of (1). The number of pairs $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ now becomes $\asymp L^2/t^2$, which ends up costing us another acceptable factor of $x^{o(1)}$. Overall, it remains to bound a sum of the form \begin{equation} \sum_{\ell_1,\ell_2 \sim L}\, \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_{d,\ell_1,\ell_2} \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(j\omega\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; k\right), \end{equation} for some fixed $\omega \in \mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$ (independent of $\ell_1, \ell_2$). Using \cref{thm:di-type-bound}, we obtain a bound like \cref{eq:sketch-final-bound} where the factor depending on $\theta_{\max}$ is \[ \left(\frac{NL}{L^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} \approx x^{\left(\frac{1}{5}-3\sigma\right) \theta_{\max}}, \] rather than $x^{\theta_{\max}/2}$. Thus instead of \cref{eq:sketch-sigma}, we now reach the desired bound provided that \[ \left(4 - 3\theta_{\max}\right)\sigma < \frac{1}{10} - \frac{\theta_{\max}}{5}, \] which is possible since $(1/5) \cdot (7/32) = 0.04375 < 0.1$. In fact, this handles all values \[ \sigma < \frac{1-2\theta_{\max}}{40-30\theta_{\max}} \qquad\qquad \iff \qquad\qquad \frac{3}{5} + \sigma < \frac{5-4\theta_{\max}}{8-6\theta_{\max}}, \] reaching the exponent of distribution in \cref{eq:exponent-theta}. Plugging in Kim--Sarnak's bound of $\theta_{\max} \le 7/32$ (\cref{thm:kim-sarnak}) yields the unconditional exponent of $66/107 \approx 0.617$ from \cref{thm:distribution-simplified}. \begin{remark} It is likely that optimized Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds like \cref{thm:di-kloosterman} could also improve Drappeau's argument \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}, leading to a triple convolution estimate with different ranges than in our \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}. In terms of the final exponent of distribution of smooth numbers, all such methods currently seem limited below $66/107$ unconditionally (and $5/8$ conditionally). \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Fixing $t$ and $\ell_i$ mod $t$ makes coefficients level-independent, so Theorem 3.9 applies and gives exponent $(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta)$.

nodes.name: Power savings and deamplification
nodes.statement: To increase the range of uniformity in $y$, we adapt Drappeau's version of the dispersion method \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}: we aim for a triple convolution estimate with a power-saving in \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}, after separating the contribution of small-conductor Dirichlet characters \[ \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{r} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\varepsilon}} \chi(mn\ell) \] from \cref{eq:sketch-triple-conv}; this can be handled via \cref{lem:harper}. As a result, the simpler two dispersion sums $\mathcal{S}_2$, $\mathcal{S}_3$ and their main terms involve Dirichlet characters (see \cref{prop:setup,prop:main-terms}), which ultimately bring in the classical Gauss sum bound (\cref{lem:gauss}) and the multiplicative large sieve (\cref{lem:large-sieve}). The difficulties in working with a general residue $a_1 \overline{a_2}$ for $a_1, a_2 \ll x^\delta$, and in obtaining power savings throughout the computations in \cref{subsec:limitations}, are quite tedious but purely technical (following \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}). We also adapt a ``deamplification'' argument of Maynard \cite{maynard2020primes}, which introduces an artificial sum over $e \sim E = x^{o(1)}$ into the dispersion sums (by averaging over the residue of $n\ell \pmod{e}$ before applying Cauchy--Schwarz); for instance, the sum in \cref{eq:sketch-main-exponential} becomes \[ \sum_{e \sim E}\, \sum_{r \sim R}\, \sum_{k \sim NL} u_k \sum_{n \sim N} \beta_n \sum_{\substack{\ell \sim L \\ n\ell \equiv k \pmod{re}}} \gamma_\ell \sum_{h \sim R/M} \textnormal{e}\left(h \frac{\overline{k}}{r} \right). \] Keeping $e$ inside the second application of Cauchy--Schwarz, this essentially reduces the contribution of the diagonal terms in \cref{eq:sketch-diagonal-terms} by a factor of $E$, allowing us to cover wider ranges of sequence lengths in \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} (including the case $M = N$). This is generally convenient, and critical when one has less control over the sizes of the sequence lengths (which is the case in applications to the primes, but not to smooth numbers).
nodes.statement_short: Drappeau's character-separation and Maynard's deamplification complete the argument.

nodes.name: Strategy via level-averaged DI bounds
nodes.statement: Starting from the work of Deshouillers--Iwaniec \cite{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, better bounds (in the $\theta$-aspect) for sums like \cref{eq:sketch-kloosterman} have been available when one additionally averages over the level $\ell_1\ell_2$, and at least one of the sequences of coefficients is independent of the level. Indeed, Drappeau's triple convolution estimate \cite{drappeau2015theoremes} and prior works rely on \cite[Theorem 12]{deshouillers1982kloosterman}, which gives such a result for incomplete Kloosterman sums. Following Maynard's argument (which is in turn based on Bombieri--Friedlander--Iwaniec's work in \cite[\S 10]{bombieri1987primes2}), we prefer to complete our Kloosterman sums, bound the contribution from the zeroth Fourier coefficient by hand, and separate into terms with $\ell_1 = \ell_2$ and $\ell_1 \neq \ell_2$, all before invoking Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds. We then aim to apply an optimized bound for sums of complete Kloosterman sums with averaging over the level (given in \cref{thm:di-type-bound}), which improves \cite[Theorem 11]{deshouillers1982kloosterman} by making the dependence on the $\theta_{\max}$ parameter explicit. But for this strategy to work out, we would need: \begin{itemize} \item
nodes.statement_short: Plan: complete Kloosterman sums and use an optimized level-averaged DI bound.

nodes.name: Requirement (1): dense range
nodes.statement: [(1).] The range of $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum} to be (discretely) dense inside $[L, 2L]^2$, and \item
nodes.statement_short: Need $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$ dense in $[L,2L]^2$.

nodes.name: Requirement (2): level-independent coefficients
nodes.statement: [(2).] Crucially, the coefficients $e\left(j \overline{\ell_1} / t \right)$ to not depend on $\ell_1, \ell_2$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Need coefficients independent of $\ell_1,\ell_2$.

nodes.name: Fix t and residues
nodes.statement: While (2) is obviously false in our case, it is only barely false for the specific ranges in \cref{eq:sketch-ranges}, due to the smallness of the parameter $t \sim x^\delta$. In particular, losing a factor of at most $x^{O(\delta)} = x^{o(1)}$ in \cref{eq:sketch-final-sum}, we may fix $t$ and the values of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2 \pmod{t}$, turning (2) into a true statement at the expense of (1). The number of pairs $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ now becomes $\asymp L^2/t^2$, which ends up costing us another acceptable factor of $x^{o(1)}$. Overall, it remains to bound a sum of the form \begin{equation} \sum_{\ell_1,\ell_2 \sim L}\, \sum_{d \sim RL/M} a_{d,\ell_1,\ell_2} \sum_{j \sim x^\delta L} \textnormal{e}\left(j\omega\right) \sum_{k \sim NL} S\left(d \overline{\ell_1 \ell_2}, j; k\right), \end{equation} for some fixed $\omega \in \mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z}$ (independent of $\ell_1, \ell_2$). Using \cref{thm:di-type-bound}, we obtain a bound like \cref{eq:sketch-final-bound} where the factor depending on $\theta_{\max}$ is \[ \left(\frac{NL}{L^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} \approx x^{\left(\frac{1}{5}-3\sigma\right) \theta_{\max}}, \] rather than $x^{\theta_{\max}/2}$. Thus instead of \cref{eq:sketch-sigma}, we now reach the desired bound provided that \[ \left(4 - 3\theta_{\max}\right)\sigma < \frac{1}{10} - \frac{\theta_{\max}}{5}, \] which is possible since $(1/5) \cdot (7/32) = 0.04375 < 0.1$. In fact, this handles all values \[ \sigma < \frac{1-2\theta_{\max}}{40-30\theta_{\max}} \qquad\qquad \iff \qquad\qquad \frac{3}{5} + \sigma < \frac{5-4\theta_{\max}}{8-6\theta_{\max}}, \] reaching the exponent of distribution in \cref{eq:exponent-theta}. Plugging in Kim--Sarnak's bound of $\theta_{\max} \le 7/32$ (\cref{thm:kim-sarnak}) yields the unconditional exponent of $66/107 \approx 0.617$ from \cref{thm:distribution-simplified}. \begin{remark} It is likely that optimized Deshouillers--Iwaniec-style bounds like \cref{thm:di-kloosterman} could also improve Drappeau's argument \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}, leading to a triple convolution estimate with different ranges than in our \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}. In terms of the final exponent of distribution of smooth numbers, all such methods currently seem limited below $66/107$ unconditionally (and $5/8$ conditionally). \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Fixing $t$ and $\ell_i$ mod $t$ makes (2) true at small cost, giving the improved exponent.

nodes.name: Fix parameters and reduce
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be sufficiently small, let $C$ be the maximum between $\varepsilon^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}$ and the constant $C$ given by \cref{lem:harper}, and let $(\log x)^C \le y \le x^{1/C}$, $D := x^\varepsilon$, $\theta := \theta_{\max}$. Up to a scaling of $\varepsilon$, we want to show that \cref{eq:exponent} holds for the range of moduli \[ r \le x^{\alpha}, \qquad\qquad {\alpha} := \frac{5-4\theta}{8-6\theta} - 1000 \varepsilon, \] and we note that error terms of the form $O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\delta})$ are acceptable in \cref{eq:exponent} (up to slightly modifying the value of $\delta$), due to the inequality $x^{1-\delta} \ll \Psi(x, y) y^{-\delta/2}$ (see \cite[p.\ 856]{drappeau2015theoremes}). We may of course assume that $a_1$ and $a_2$ are relatively prime, by reducing any common factors.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\varepsilon$, $C$, $D=x^\varepsilon$; reduce to coprime $a_1,a_2$.

nodes.name: Separate small-conductor characters
nodes.statement: We split the left-hand side of \cref{eq:exponent} into \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{n\overline{a_1}a_2 \equiv 1 \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(n,r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} \right) \bigg\vert \\ &\le \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert + \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(n,r)=1}}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ prim.},\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le D}} \chi(n\overline{a_1}a_2) \bigg\vert. \end{aligned} \] The second sum is just \[ \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \bigg\vert \sum_{n \in S(x, y)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{r} \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le D}} \chi(n) \bigg\vert , \] which is appropriately bounded by \cref{lem:harper} and the triangle inequality. It remains to bound the first sum.
nodes.statement_short: Split off small-conductor characters and bound them by Lemma 3.2.

nodes.name: Discard small n, dyadic decomposition
nodes.statement: Note that the range $n \in S(x, y)$ means $n \le x$ and $P^+(n) \le y$, where $P^+(n)$ denotes the greatest prime factor of $n$. We bound the contribution of $n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon}$ trivially, as in \cite[p.\ 855]{drappeau2015theoremes}: \[ \sum_{\substack{r \le x^{\alpha} \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon} \\ P^+(n) \le y}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert \ll_\varepsilon x^{\alpha} + \sum_{\substack{n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon} \\ a_2 n \neq a_1}} \tau(|a_2n - a_1|) + x^{\varepsilon/2} \sum_{n \ll x^{1-\varepsilon}} 1 \ll_\varepsilon x^{1-\varepsilon/2}, \] and put the other $n$'s into $O(\log x)$ dyadic ranges $n \sim X$, with $x^{1-\varepsilon} \le X \ll x$. We also extend the range of $r$ in these sums to $r \le X^{{\alpha} + 10\varepsilon}$, noting that $x^{\alpha} \le x^{(1-\varepsilon)({\alpha} + 10\varepsilon)}$. Putting $r$ into $O(\log x)$ dyadic ranges $r \sim R$, it remains to bound sums of the form \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{n \sim X \\ P^+(n) \le y}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert, \end{equation} for $R \ll X^{{\alpha}+10\varepsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $n\ll x^{1-\varepsilon}$ trivially and reduce to dyadic sums (4.5).

nodes.name: Bombieri–Vinogradov range
nodes.statement: The contribution of the Bombieri--Vinogradov range $R \ll X^{(1/2) - (\varepsilon/10)}$ is handled by classical methods (e.g., using \cite[Theorem 17.4]{iwaniec2021analytic}; see \cite{drappeau2015theoremes,drappeau2017smooth}).
nodes.statement_short: Small moduli are handled classically.

nodes.name: Factorize smooth numbers
nodes.statement: For any $R$ in the remaining range $X^{(1/2) - (\varepsilon/10)} \le R \ll X^{{\alpha}+10\varepsilon}$, we set \begin{equation} M_0 := \frac{X^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad N_0 := \frac{X^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad L_0 := \frac{R^2}{X^{1-20\varepsilon}}, \end{equation} and factorize smooth numbers as in \cite[Lemme 7]{drappeau2015theoremes} to rewrite the sum in \cref{eq:sum-r-to-estimate} as \[ \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2) = 1}} \bigg\vert \sum_{\substack{L_0 < \ell \le L_0 P^-(\ell) \\ P^+(\ell) \le y}} \sum_{\substack{M_0 < m \le M_0 P^-(m) \\ P^+(m) \le P^-(\ell)}} \sum_{\substack{mn\ell \sim X \\ P^+(n) \le P^-(m)}} \mathcal{E}_D(n\overline{a_1}a_2; r) \bigg\vert, \] where $P^-(n)$ denotes the smallest prime factor of $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose lengths (4.6) and factor smooth numbers as $mn\ell$.

nodes.name: Check conditions (4.2)
nodes.statement: We also put $m, n, \ell$ into $O((\log y)^3)$ dyadic ranges $m \sim M$, $n \sim N$, $\ell \sim L$, with $M \in [M_0, yM_0]$, $N \in [y^{-2}N_0, N_0]$, $L \in [L_0, yL_0]$, and $MNL \asymp X$. Recalling that $y \le x^{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)} \le X^\varepsilon$, it is easily checked that for such $M, N, L$ and $X^{(1/2)-(\varepsilon/10)} \le R \ll X^{{\alpha}+10\varepsilon} = X^{(5-4\theta)/(8-6\theta) - 990\varepsilon}$, and small enough $\varepsilon$, the conditions in \cref{eq:conditions} are satisfied (with respect to $X$ instead of $x$).
nodes.statement_short: Dyadic ranges for $m,n,\ell$ satisfy (4.2).

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: At this point, our sums are almost in the right form to apply the triple convolution estimate in \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate}, except for a few joint constraints on the variables $m, n, \ell$ (these are $P^+(m) \le P^-(\ell)$, $P^+(n) \le P^-(m)$, respectively $mn\ell \sim X$). The last step of analytically separating these constraints is identical to that in \cite[pp.\ 853--854]{drappeau2015theoremes}, except that in the end we apply \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} instead of \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 3]{drappeau2015theoremes}. Overall, the contribution of the range $X^{(1/2)-(\varepsilon/10)} \le R \ll X^{{\alpha} + 10\varepsilon}$ is $O_\varepsilon\left( (\log x)^{O(1)} x^{1-\delta} \right)$, which is acceptable; this completes our proof.
nodes.statement_short: Separate joint constraints analytically and apply Theorem 4.1.

nodes.name: Discard k divisible by e
nodes.statement: For a fixed prime $e \sim E$, we wish to eliminate the contribution to $\Delta$ of the terms $k$ with $(e, k) \neq 1$, i.e., $e \mid k$. This contribution is \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m, r) = 1} \alpha_m \sum_{\substack{e \mid k \in (K, 4K] \\ (k, r) = 1}} u_{k} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r) \right) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2e)=1}} \sum_{e \mid s \in (MK, 8MK]} x^{\varepsilon/2} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{s \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} + \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} D^2 \right) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon} \sum_{r \sim R} \left(\frac{MK}{RE} + 1 + \left(\frac{MK}{E} + 1\right) \frac{D^2}{R}\right) \quad \ll x^{\varepsilon} \left(\frac{xD^2}{E} + R + D^2\right) \ll x^{\varepsilon} \left(\frac{x^{1+2\varepsilon}}{x^{4\varepsilon}} + R + x^{2\varepsilon}\right), \end{aligned} \] which is $\ll x^{1-\varepsilon}$ since $R \ll x^{(2/3)-11\varepsilon}$ by \cref{eq:conditions}. It follows that \[ \Delta = \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m,r)=1} \alpha_m \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r) \right) + O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\varepsilon}), \] where we also made explicit the restriction $(mk, r) = 1$, required for the summand to be nonzero.
nodes.statement_short: Terms with $e\mid k$ contribute $O(x^{1-\varepsilon})$.

nodes.name: Split by residue mod re
nodes.statement: Now for fixed $m$ and $e$ we have \[ \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \mathbbm{1}_{mk \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} = \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}}, \] and there are precisely $\varphi(re)/\varphi(r)$ choices of $b$ in the summation; thus \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta &= \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m,r)=1} \alpha_m \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right) \\ &+ O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\varepsilon}). \end{aligned} \] (For a complete deamplification setup, one could also try to split the term $\omega_D(mk\overline{a_1}a_2; r)$ according to the residue $b$ of $k \pmod{re}$, but we do not need to do this in our proof.)
nodes.statement_short: Split the $k$-sum by residue class $b$ mod $re$.

nodes.name: Average over primes e
nodes.statement: We then average over $e$ in the set $\mathcal{E}$ from \cref{eq:averaging-set}, which has size $|\mathscr{E}| \asymp_\varepsilon E/\log E$ (recalling that $E \gg x^{\varepsilon}$ and $|a_2| \le x^\delta$). Thus up to an error of $O_\varepsilon(x^{1-\varepsilon})$, we can rewrite $\Delta$ as \[ \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \rho_r \sum_{(m,r)=1} \alpha_m \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Average the identity over $e\in\mathscr E$.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Schwarz
nodes.statement: We now apply Cauchy--Schwarz in the $e,r,m,b$ variables, allowing us to eliminate the $\rho_r$ and $\alpha_m$ coefficients; this gives \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} |\Delta|^2 &\ll \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|^2} \left( \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \sum_{(m,r)=1} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} |\rho_r|^2 |\alpha_m|^2 \right) \Delta' + O_\varepsilon(x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}) \\ &\ll \frac{1}{|\mathscr{E}|^2} \left( \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2)=1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ (m,r)=1}} \frac{\varphi(re)}{\varphi(r)} \right) \Delta' + O_\varepsilon(x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}) \\ &\ll_\varepsilon MR (\log E) \Delta' + x^{2(1-\varepsilon)}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where we used that $\varphi(re) \le \varphi(r) e$, and we denoted \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta' &:= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r,a_1a_2)=1}} \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ (m,r)=1}} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy–Schwarz removes $\rho_r,\alpha_m$, giving (5.7).

nodes.name: Smooth majorants and expansion
nodes.statement: Anticipating a later application of Poisson summation, we bound the indicator functions $\mathbbm{1}_{m \sim M}$ and $\mathbbm{1}_{r \sim R}$ from above by $\Phi(m/M)$ and $\Phi(r/R)$. Then we expand the square and perform the $b$-summation to obtain \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \Delta' &\le \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\substack{(r,a_1a_2)=1}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{(m,r)=1}} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2 m} \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b\ (re)} - \frac{\omega_D(mk \overline{a_1}a_2; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= M \left(\mathcal{S}_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} \mathcal{S}_2 + \mathcal{S}_3\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Insert smooth weights and expand the square to get (5.8).

nodes.name: Conclude (5.5)
nodes.statement: Combining \cref{eq:delta-squared} with \cref{eq:delta-prime} and recalling that $M \asymp x/K$, we recover \cref{eq:setup}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine (5.7) and (5.8).

nodes.name: Write main terms as a square
nodes.statement: In analogy with \cref{eq:delta-prime}, we can write \[ \begin{aligned} &X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r, a_1a_2) = 1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv c \pmod{r}}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(k\overline{c}; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &\ll \frac{1}{R} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{r} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\mathbbm{1}_{k \equiv b \pmod{re}} - \frac{\omega_D(k\overline{b}; r)}{\varphi(re)} \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= \frac{1}{R} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_r \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)^2} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) \right)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $X_1-2\mathrm{Re}X_2+X_3$ as a sum of squares.

nodes.name: Character difference set S
nodes.statement: Note that \[ \begin{aligned} \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) &= \left( \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; r) \right) + \left( \omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; r) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) \right) \\ &= \sum_{\substack{\chi \in S}} \chi(k)\overline{\chi(b)}, \end{aligned} \] where $S = S(r,e,\varepsilon) = S_1 \cup S_2$ and \[ \begin{aligned} S_1 &:= \left\{ \chi \text{ primitive} : \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \nmid r, \text{ but } \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid re \right\}, \\ S_2 &:= \left\{ \chi \text{ primitive} : \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D \text{ and } \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r \right\}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: The difference of $\omega$'s is a sum over characters in $S=S_1\cup S_2$.

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.statement: Since all the characters in $S$ are primitive, any distinct $\chi_1, \chi_2 \in S$ must induce different characters modulo $re$. Thus $\chi_1 \overline{\chi_2} \mathbbm{1}_{(re, \cdot) = 1}$ is not the principal character modulo $re$, so it must have average $0$. But then \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \left(\omega_\infty(k\overline{b}; re) - \omega_D(k\overline{b}; r) \right)\right\vert^2 \\ &= \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \left\vert \sum_{\chi \in S} \overline{\chi}(b) \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k) \right\vert^2 \\ &= \sum_{\chi_1,\chi_2 \in S} \left(\sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi_1(k)\right)\overline{\left(\sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi_2(k)\right)} \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times}} \overline{\chi_1}(b) \chi_2(b) \\ &= \varphi(re) \sum_{\chi \in S} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality of distinct characters mod $re$.

nodes.name: Reduce to conductors > D
nodes.statement: We conclude that \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 \ &\ll \frac{1}{R}\sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_r \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{\chi \in S} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2 \\ &\le \frac{1}{R}\sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_r \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid re}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2, \end{aligned} \] where we used that all characters $\chi \in S_1$ also have $\textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D$, since $D \le x^\varepsilon < E \le e \mid \textnormal{cond}(\chi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound by characters of conductor $>D$ dividing $re$.

nodes.name: Substitute q = re
nodes.statement: Now letting $Q := RE$, substituting $q$ for $re$, and using that $q$ has $O(\log q)$ different prime factors, we can bound the sum above by \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 &\ll \frac{\log x}{R}\sum_{Q/2 \le q \le 6Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) > D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid q}} \left\vert \sum_{(k,q)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2. \\ &\le \frac{\log x}{R} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}}\, \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ s \mid q}} \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \left\vert \sum_{(k,q/s)=1} u_k \chi(k)\right\vert^2 \\ &\le \frac{\log x}{R} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}}\, \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ s \mid q}} \frac{\tau(q/s)}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{d \mid q/s} \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(dk')\right\vert^2 \\ &\le \frac{\log x}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}}\, \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(k')\right\vert^2 \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ ds \mid q}} \frac{\tau(q/s)}{\varphi(q)}, \end{aligned} \] where we decomposed $\mathbbm{1}_{(a, b) = 1} = \sum_{d \mid (a, b)} \mu(d)$ to get rid of the coprimality restriction.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $q=re$ and remove coprimality by Möbius.

nodes.name: Sum over q
nodes.statement: Noting that \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le 6Q \\ sd \mid q}} \frac{\tau(q/s)}{\varphi(q)} \le \sum_{\substack{q' \le 6Q}} \frac{\tau(q'd)}{\varphi(q'ds)} \le \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)\varphi(s)} \sum_{\substack{q' \le 6Q}} \frac{\tau(q')}{\varphi(q')} \ll \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)\varphi(s)} (\log x)^2, \] we further have \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2\textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 &\ll \frac{(\log x)^3}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)} \sum_{D < s \le 6Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(s)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}} \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(k')\right\vert^2 \\ &= \frac{(\log x)^3}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)}{\varphi(d)} \int_D^\infty \sum_{D < s \le \min(6Q, t)} \frac{s}{\varphi(s)} \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) = s}} \left\vert \sum_{k'} u_{dk'} \chi(k')\right\vert^2 \frac{dt}{t^2}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound the $q$-sum by $(\log x)^2\tau(d)/(\varphi(d)\varphi(s))$.

nodes.name: Apply large sieve
nodes.statement: Finally, applying the multiplicative large sieve from \cref{lem:large-sieve} as in \cite[p.\ 900]{drappeau2017smooth} (see also the top of \cite[p.\ 852]{drappeau2015theoremes}, which misses a factor of $(\tau(d) \log K)^2$), we conclude that \[ \begin{aligned} X_1 - 2 \textnormal{Re} X_2 + X_3 &\ll \frac{(\log x)^2}{R} \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)}{d\varphi(d)} \int_D^\infty \left(\frac{K}{d} + \min(6Q, t)^2 \right) \sum_{k' \asymp K/d} |u_{dk'}|^2\ \frac{dt}{t^2} \\ &\ll \frac{(\log x)^3}{R} K (\log K)^3 \sum_{d \le 6Q} \frac{\tau(d)^3}{d\varphi(d)} \left( \frac{K}{dD} + Q \right) \\ &\ll (\log x)^6 \frac{K}{R} \left(\frac{K}{D} + Q\right) \\ &\ll (\log x)^6 K^2 (RD)^{-1}, \end{aligned} \] as we wanted. In the last line, we made use of the condition $RE \ll x^{-\varepsilon}K$ (from \cref{eq:E-conditions}) to bound $Q = RE \ll K/D$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicative large sieve (Lemma 3.3) gives the bound.

nodes.name: Choose E
nodes.statement: The hypothesis of \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} assumes \cref{eq:conditions}, so we can pick $E$ as in \cref{prop:dispersion-sums}.$(i)$, subject to \cref{eq:E-conditions}.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $E$ from Proposition 6.2(i).

nodes.name: Combine propositions
nodes.statement: Then, by combining \cref{prop:setup,prop:dispersion-sums,prop:main-terms}, we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta &\ll_\varepsilon x\sqrt{\frac{R\log x}{K^2} \left(\widehat{\Phi}(0)\frac{K^2}{RD}(\log x)^6 + x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R} \right)} + x^{1-\varepsilon} \\ &\ll x\sqrt{(\log x)^7 \left(\frac{1}{D} + \frac{1}{x^{2\delta}}\right)} + x^{1-\varepsilon} \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Combine Propositions 5.1, 6.1, 6.2.

nodes.name: Adjust delta
nodes.statement: The conclusion of \cref{thm:triple-conv-estimate} follows after replacing $\delta$ with $\min(\delta, \varepsilon)$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\delta$ by $\min(\delta,\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Expand S_3 difference
nodes.statement: Recall from \cref{eq:sums-2} that \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_3 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \left\vert \sum_{(k,re)=1} u_k \sum_{\substack{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k \overline{a_1}a_2 c)\right\vert^2 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re)} \sum_{\substack{\chi_1, \chi_2 \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi_i) \mid r}} \overline{\chi_1} \chi_2 (a_1 \overline{a_2}) \sum_{\substack{k_1, k_2 \\ (k_1k_2, re) = 1}} \chi_1(k_1) u_{k_1} \overline{\chi_2(k_2) u_{k_2}} \\ & \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad \times \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c) \mathcal{E}_r(c), \end{aligned} \] where $\mathcal{E}_r(c)$ is given by \cref{eq:Poisson-difference}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\mathcal S_3-\hat\Phi(0)X_3$ over characters.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Truncated Poisson
nodes.statement: Expanding $\mathcal{E}_r(c)$ according to \cref{lem:poisson} with $H := x^\varepsilon R M^{-1}$, we obtain \begin{equation} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c) \mathcal{E}_r(c) = \frac{1}{r} \sum_{0 < |h| < H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c)\ \textnormal{e}\left(\frac{ch}{r}\right) + O_\varepsilon\left(x^{-100}\right). \end{equation} (In such manipulations, we warn the reader of the potential confusion between the integer variable $e \in \mathscr{E}$ and the function $\textnormal{e}(\cdot)$; the difference should be clear from context.)
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\mathcal E_r(c)$ by Lemma 3.4, giving Gauss sums (7.1).
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Gauss sum bound
nodes.statement: The inner sum (over $c$) in \cref{eq:Gauss} is a Gauss sum, which we can bound using \cref{lem:gauss} for the Dirichlet character $\chi_1 \overline{\chi_2} \mathbbm{1}_{(\cdot, r) = 1} \pmod{r}$ (whose conductor divides $r$ and is at most equal to $D^2 \le x^{2\varepsilon}$). This yields \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \chi_1 \overline{\chi_2}(c) \mathcal{E}_r(c) &\ll_\varepsilon x^{-100} + \frac{1}{r} \sum_{0 < |h| < H} x^\varepsilon \sum_{d \mid (h, r)} d \\ &\ll x^{-100} + \frac{x^\varepsilon}{r} \sum_{d \mid r} d \sum_{0 < |h| < H/d} 1 \ll \frac{x^{\varepsilon}}{R} \tau(r) H = x^{2\varepsilon} \frac{\tau(r)}{M}, \end{aligned} \] which leads to \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_3 \ll_\varepsilon x^{2\varepsilon} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{\tau(r)}{\varphi(r)\varphi(re) M} |\mathcal{X}_D|^2 K^2 &\ll x^{6\varepsilon} \frac{K^2}{M} \sum_{r} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{\tau(r)}{\varphi(r)^2} \\ &\ll x^{6\varepsilon} \frac{K^2}{MR} (\log R)^{O(1)}, \end{aligned} \] using that $\varphi(re) \gg \varphi(r) e$ (since $e$ is prime).
nodes.statement_short: Bound the Gauss sums by Lemma 3.6 and sum up.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $x/M \asymp K \ll x^{(2/3)-6\varepsilon}$ by \cref{eq:conditions}, we have $M \gg x^{1/3+6\varepsilon} \gg x^{7\varepsilon}$ for small enough $\varepsilon$, and in particular $\mathcal{S}_3 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_3\ll_\varepsilon x^{-\varepsilon} K^2/R$, proving the easier third of \cref{prop:dispersion-sums}.
nodes.statement_short: Since $M\gg x^{7\varepsilon}$, the bound is $x^{-\varepsilon}K^2/R$.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Expand S_2 difference
nodes.statement: Recall from \cref{eq:sums-2} that \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{S}_2 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_2 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} \mathcal{E}_r(c) \sum_{\substack{(k_1k_2,re)=1 \\ k_2 \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \sum_{\substack{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k_1 \overline{a_1} a_2 c) \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D} \sum_{(k_1 k_2, e) = 1} \chi(k_1) u_{k_1} \overline{\chi(k_2) u_{k_2}} \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} \mathcal{E}_r(a_1 \overline{a_2 k_2}). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\mathcal S_2-\hat\Phi(0)X_2$ over characters.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Truncated Poisson
nodes.statement: Applying \cref{lem:poisson} with $H := x^\varepsilon R M^{-1}$ to expand $\mathcal{E}_r(a_1\overline{a_2 k_2})$ (as given in \cref{eq:Poisson-difference}), we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{S}_2 - \widehat{\Phi}(0) X_2 \\ &= \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D} \sum_{(k_1 k_2, e) = 1} \chi(k_1) u_{k_1} \overline{\chi(k_2) u_{k_2}} \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \frac{1}{r\varphi(re)} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{a_1 h \overline{a_2k_2}}{r}\right) \\ &+ O_\varepsilon\left(x^{-90}\right), \end{aligned} \] where we used that $\varphi(re) \gg \varphi(r) e$ as before (since $e$ is prime).
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\mathcal E_r$ by Lemma 3.4.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Focus on Y_2
nodes.statement: The error term is acceptable, so let us focus on the main term in the right-hand side (denote this by $Y_2$).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the main term $Y_2$.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Bézout reciprocity
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:bezout}, we have \[ \frac{\overline{a_2 k_2}}{r} + \frac{\overline{r}}{a_2 k_2} \equiv \frac{1}{a_2 k_2 r} \quad \pmod{1}, \] so that \begin{equation} Y_2 \ll \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{\chi \in \mathcal{X}_D} \sum_{k_1, k_2} |u_{k_1} u_{k_2}| \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \frac{1}{r\varphi(re)} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e} \left(\frac{a_1 h}{a_2 k_2 r} - \frac{a_1 h\overline{r}}{a_2 k_2}\right) \right\vert. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Flip the modulus by Bézout, giving (7.2).
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Decompose 1/phi(re)
nodes.statement: At this point we decompose \[ \frac{1}{\varphi(re)} = \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \left(\frac{1}{e-1} - \frac{1}{e(e-1)} \mathbbm{1}_{e \mid r} \right), \] aiming to apply the exponential sum bound in \cref{lem:incomplete-weil}. Fixing $e, a_i, k_i, h$, this lets us rewrite the sum over $r$ in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:Y2} as \[ \frac{1}{e-1} Z_2(\textnormal{cond}(\chi)) - \frac{1}{e(e-1)} Z_2([\textnormal{cond}(\chi), e]), \] where \[ Z_2(\ell) := \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i)=1 \\ \ell \mid r}} u(r) \frac{r}{\varphi(r)}\ \textnormal{e} \left(-\frac{a_1 h\overline{r}}{a_2k_2} \right) \] and \[ u(r) := \frac{1}{r^2} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e} \left( \frac{a_1h}{a_2k_2 r} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $1/\varphi(re)$ and define $Z_2$, $u(r)$.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Derivative bounds for u
nodes.statement: Note that $u$ extends to a differentiable function of a real variable $\xi$, supported in $[R/2, 3R/2]$, and with derivative bounds \[ \begin{aligned} |u'(\xi)| &\ll \frac{1}{R^3} + \frac{1}{R^2} \left(\frac{1}{R} + \frac{HM}{R^2} + \frac{|a_1| H}{KR^2} \right) \\ &\ll \frac{1}{R^2} \left(\frac{1}{R} + \frac{x^\varepsilon R}{R^2} + \frac{|a_1| x^\varepsilon R}{xR^2} \right) \quad \ll \frac{x^{2\varepsilon}}{R^3}. \end{aligned} \] in this region (we used that $H = x^\varepsilon R M^{-1}$, $MK \asymp x$, and the very crude bound $|a_1| \ll x^{1+\varepsilon}$).
nodes.statement_short: Bound $u'$ by $x^{2\varepsilon}/R^3$.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Partial summation and incomplete Weil
nodes.statement: So we may use integration by parts to estimate $Z_2$; letting \[ v_\ell(\xi) := \sum_{\substack{(r, a_ik_i) = 1 \\ \ell \mid r \le \xi}} \frac{r}{\varphi(r)}\ \textnormal{e} \left(- \frac{a_1 h\overline{r}}{a_2k_2} \right), \] which can be bounded via \cref{lem:incomplete-weil} (with $n = a_1 h$, $c = a_2k_2$, $d = r$ and $k = a_1k_1$), we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} Z_2(\ell) = \int u(\xi) dv_\ell(\xi) = - \int v_\ell(\xi) du(\xi) &\ll \frac{x^{2\varepsilon}}{R^2} \sup_{\xi \in [R/2, 3R]} |v_\ell(\xi)| \\ &\ll_\varepsilon \frac{x^{3\varepsilon}}{R^2} \left((a_1 h, a_2 k_2)^{1/2}K^{1/2} + (a_1 h, a_2 k_2) \frac{R}{K} \right), \end{aligned} \] uniformly in $\ell \ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts and apply Lemma 3.8.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Sum up
nodes.statement: Returning to \cref{eq:Y2} and summing over $h$ and $k_2$, the GCD-terms contribute at most $O_\varepsilon(x^{\varepsilon})$ on average (since $(a_1, a_2) = 1$). Thus \[ \begin{aligned} Y_2 \ll_\varepsilon x^{4\varepsilon} |\mathscr{E}| |\chi_D| K^2 H \frac{1}{E} \frac{1}{R^2} \left(\sqrt{K} + \frac{R}{K} \right) &\le x^{7\varepsilon} \frac{K^2}{MR} \left(\sqrt{K} + \frac{R}{K} \right) \\ &\ll x^{7\varepsilon - 1} \left(\frac{K^{7/2}}{R} + K^2\right). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Sum over $h,k_2$ to bound $Y_2$.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By \cref{eq:conditions}, we have $K^{3/2} \ll x^{1-9\varepsilon}$ and $R \ll x^{1-11\varepsilon}$, so we get a final bound of $Y_2 \ll_\varepsilon x^{-\varepsilon} K^2 / R$. This completes our proof of \cref{prop:dispersion-sums}.$(ii)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (4.2) give $Y_2\ll x^{-\varepsilon}K^2/R$.
nodes.section: 7 The second and third dispersion sums

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: We eliminate the contribution of several sets of pairs $(k_1, k_2)$, putting absolute values on all the coefficients involved; thus it does not matter if some of these eliminated sets have nonempty intersections.
nodes.statement_short: Remove several sets of pairs, with absolute values.

nodes.name: Almost-diagonal pairs
nodes.statement: First, we consider the almost-diagonal pairs with $|k_1 - k_2| \le K/x^\eta$, which contribute to $\mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1$ at most \[ \begin{aligned} &\ll \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} |\mathcal{E}_r(c)| \sum_{\substack{k_1 \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2c} \pmod{r} \\ (k_1, e) = 1}} |u_{k_1}| \sum_{\substack{k_2 \equiv k_1 \pmod{re} \\ |k_1 - k_2| \le K/x^\eta}} |u_{k_2}| \\ &\ll_\eta x^{\eta/2} E R \left(\frac{K}{R} + 1\right) \left(\frac{K}{x^\eta RE} + 1\right) \\ &\ll_\eta x^{\eta/2}ER \frac{K}{R} \frac{K}{x^\eta RE} \\ &\asymp x^{-\eta/2} \frac{K^2}{R}, \end{aligned} \] where we used that $\sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} |\mathcal{E}_r(c)| \le \frac{1}{M} \sum_m \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) + \widehat{\Phi}(0) \ll 1$, and that $x^{\eta} RE \ll K$ (which follows from \cref{eq:E-conditions} and $\eta \le \varepsilon$).
nodes.statement_short: Pairs with $|k_1-k_2|\le K/x^\eta$ contribute $x^{-\eta/2}K^2/R$.

nodes.name: Pairs with large gcd
nodes.statement: Then, we consider those pairs with $v := (k_1, k_2) > x^{\eta/2}$. Their contribution to $\mathcal{S}_1 - \widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1$ is at most \[ \ll \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} |\mathcal{E}_r(c)| \sum_{\substack{b \in (\mathbf{Z}/re\mathbf{Z})^\times \\ b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} \sum_{\substack{v > x^{\eta/2} \\ (v,re)=1}} \left(\sum_{\substack{k \equiv b \pmod{re} \\ v \mid k}} |u_k| \right)^2. \] Using that $(v, re) = 1$, we can bound one inner sum over $k$ by $\ll_\eta x^{\eta/8}(K(vRE)^{-1} + 1) \ll x^{-3\eta/8}K(RE)^{-1}$ (recall that $x^{\eta} RE \ll K$ by \cref{eq:E-conditions}). This yields a total contribution of \[ \begin{aligned} &\ll_\eta \frac{K}{REx^{3\eta/8}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} |\mathcal{E}_r(c)| \sum_{\substack{v > x^\eta \\ (v,re)=1}} \sum_{\substack{k \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r} \\ v \mid k}} |u_k| \\ &\le \frac{K}{Rx^{3\eta/8}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{c \in (\mathbf{Z}/r\mathbf{Z})^\times} |\mathcal{E}_r(c)| \sum_{\substack{k \equiv a_1\overline{a_2c} \pmod{r}}} \tau(k) |u_k| \\ &\ll_\eta \frac{K}{Rx^{2\eta/8}} R \left(\frac{K}{R} + 1\right) \\ &\ll x^{-\eta/4} \frac{K^2}{R}, \end{aligned} \] which is also acceptable.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs with $(k_1,k_2)>x^{\eta/2}$ contribute $x^{-\eta/4}K^2/R$.

nodes.name: Pairs with large d_1 or d_2
nodes.statement: Keeping the notation $v = (k_1, k_2)$, which we may now assume is at most $x^{\eta/2}$, note that \[ d_1 := (k_1, (a_2k_2)^\infty) = (k_1, (a_2 v)^\infty), \] and let us consider those pairs $(k_1, k_2)$ with $d_1 > x^\eta$. These contribute to $\mathcal{S}_1$ at most \[ \begin{aligned} &\ll \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m, r) = 1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_1 \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{k_1 \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2m} \pmod{r} \\ (k_1, re) = 1,\ d_1 \mid k_1}} |u_{k_1}| \sum_{\substack{k_2 \equiv k_1 \pmod{re} \\ (k_1, k_2) = v}} |u_{k_2}| \\ &\ll_\eta x^{\eta/8} \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m, r) = 1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_1 \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, re) = 1,\ d_1 \mid k_1 \\ r \mid a_2 m k_1 - a_1}} \left(\frac{K}{REv} + 1\right) \\ &\ll x^{\eta/8} \frac{K}{RE} \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \frac{1}{v} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{m} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_1 \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{d_1 \mid k_1}} \sum_{\substack{(r,m a_1a_2)=1 \\ r \mid a_2 m k_1 - a_1}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right), \end{aligned} \] where we used that $x^{\eta/2} RE \ll K$ and swapped sums. Considering the cases $a_2 m k_1 = a_1$ and $a_2 m k_1 - a_1 \neq 0$ separately, this is further bounded by \[ \begin{aligned} &\ll x^{\eta/8} \frac{K}{RE} \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \frac{1}{v} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \left(\tau(|a_1|)^2 R + \sum_{m} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_1 \mid (a_2v)^\infty \\ d_1 \le 4K}} \sum_{\substack{d_1 \mid k_1 \\ a_2 m k_1 \neq a_1}} \tau(|a_2 m k_1 - a_1|) \right) \\ &\ll_\eta x^{\eta/4}K + x^{\eta/4} \frac{K}{RE} \max_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{m} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_1 \mid (a_2v)^\infty \\ d_1 \le 4K}} \left(\frac{K}{d_1} + 1\right) \\ &\ll x^{\eta/4}K + x^{1 + \eta/4} \frac{K}{R} \max_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_1 \le 4K \\ d_1 \mid (a_2 v)^\infty }} \frac{K}{d_1} \\ &\ll_\eta x^{-\eta/4} \frac{K^2}{R}, \end{aligned} \] where we used that $K \gg x^{\varepsilon} \gg x^\eta$, $R \ll x^{1-\eta/2}$ (by \cref{eq:conditions}), and the majorization \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d \le 4K \\ d \mid b^\infty }} d^{-1} \le x^{-2\eta/3} \sum_{\substack{d \le 4K \\ d \mid b^\infty }} d^{-1/3} = x^{-2\eta/3} O(1)^{O(\log b / \log \log b)} \ll_\eta x^{-\eta/2}, \end{equation} which holds uniformly for $b \ll x$. The contribution of the pairs with $d_1 > x^\eta$ to $\widehat{\Phi}(0)X_1$ is simpler and similarly bounded, and the contribution of the pairs with $d_2 := (k_2, (a_2k_1)^\infty) = (k_2, (a_2v)^\infty)$ is bounded symmetrically.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs with large $d_1$ (or $d_2$) are bounded via the harmonic-divisor majorization (8.2).

nodes.name: Pairs with large d_Delta
nodes.statement: All that is left is to eliminate the contribution of the pairs with large values of $(k_1 - k_2, (a_2k_1k_2)^\infty)$; since $(k_1 - k_2, k_1k_2) = (k_1 - k_2, v^2)$, we have \[ d_\Delta := (k_1 - k_2, (a_2k_1k_2)^\infty) = (k_1 - k_2, (a_2v)^\infty), \] and the pairs with $d_\Delta > x^\eta$ (as well as $v \le x^{\eta/2}$ and $|k_1 - k_2| > K/x^\eta$) contribute to $\mathcal{S}_1$ at most \[ \begin{aligned} &\ll \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{k_1 \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2m} \pmod{r} \\ (k_1, re) = 1,\ (k_1, k) = v \\ 0 < |k| \le 8K \\ [d_\Delta, re] \mid k}} |u_{k_1}u_{(k_1+k)}| \\ &\ll_\eta x^{\eta/8} \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{0 < |k| \le 8K \\ [d_\Delta, re] \mid k}} \sum_{\substack{k_1 \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2m} \pmod{r} \\ (k_1, re) = 1,\ (k_1, k) = v}} 1 \\ &\ll x^{\eta/8} \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r,a_1a_2)=1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{(m,r)=1} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{0 < |k| \le 8K \\ [d_\Delta, re] \mid k}} \left(\frac{K}{Rv} + 1\right) \\ &\ll x^{\eta/8} \frac{K}{R} \sum_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \frac{1}{v} \sum_{m} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \sum_{\substack{0 < |k| \le 8K \\ d_\Delta \mid k}} \sum_{\substack{e \in \mathscr{E} \\ (r,a_1a_2)=1 \\ re \mid k}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right), \end{aligned} \] using that $Rx^{\eta/2} \ll K$. Bounding the inner sum by $\tau(k)^2 \ll_\eta x^{\eta/9}$, this further becomes \[ \begin{aligned} &\ll_\eta x^{\eta/4} \frac{K}{R} \max_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{m} \frac{1}{M} \Phi\left(\frac{m}{M}\right) \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty \\ d_\Delta \le 8K}} \sum_{\substack{|k| \le 8K \\ d_\Delta \mid k}} 1 \\ &\ll x^{\eta/4} \frac{K}{R} \max_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty \\ d_\Delta \le 8K}} \left(\frac{K}{d_\Delta} + 1 \right) \\ &\ll x^{\eta/4} \frac{K}{R} \max_{v \le x^{\eta/2}} \sum_{\substack{x^\eta < d_\Delta \mid (a_2 v)^\infty \\ d_\Delta \le 8K}} \frac{K}{d_\Delta} \qquad\quad \ll_\eta x^{-\eta/4} \frac{K^2}{R}, \end{aligned} \] using the same majorization as in \cref{eq:harmonic-divisors}.
nodes.statement_short: Pairs with large $(k_1-k_2,(a_2v)^\infty)$ are bounded similarly.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The contribution of the pairs with $d_\Delta > x^\eta$ to $\widehat{\Phi}(0) X_1$ is simpler and similarly bounded by $O_\eta(x^{-\eta/4} K^2/R)$. Having eliminated the absolute contribution of all pairs in $\mathcal{K}(\eta)$ at least once, while incurring only admissible errors, this completes our proof of \cref{prop:bad-pairs}.
nodes.statement_short: All bad pairs removed with admissible error.

nodes.name: Reduce via Proposition 8.2
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$ be sufficiently small, and let us pick $E$ as in \cref{prop:drappeau-expo}. By \cref{prop:simplification}, it remains to establish the bound \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{D}_1 := \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r, a_1a_2) = 1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, k_2) \in \mathcal{K}(\eta) \\ (k_1 k_2, re) = 1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a_1 h \frac{\overline{a_2k_1}}{r} \right) \\ \ll_{\varepsilon,\eta} x^{-2\delta} \frac{K^2}{R}, \end{aligned} \] for some choice of $0 < 8\delta \le \eta \le \varepsilon$ in terms of $\varepsilon$ (since $\delta \le \eta/8$, the error term of $x^{-\eta/4} K^2 / R$ from \cref{prop:simplification} is acceptable). For now, let us fix $\delta$ and $\eta$ such that $8\delta \le \eta$; we will give explicit choices at the end of this proof.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $E$ and reduce to bounding the sum in Proposition 8.2.

nodes.name: Bounded gcd variables
nodes.statement: By the definition of $\mathcal{K}(\eta)$ from \cref{eq:bad-pairs}, we may consider the $x^{\eta}$-bounded variables \[ d_1 := (k_1, (a_2 k_2)^\infty), \qquad d_2 := (k_2, (a_2 k_1)^\infty), \qquad d_\Delta := (k_1 - k_2, (a_2 k_1 k_2)^\infty), \] \begin{equation} v := (k_1, k_2) = (d_1, d_2) = (d_1, d_\Delta) = (d_2, d_\Delta). \end{equation} Noting that $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\Delta$ all divide $(a_2 v)^\infty$, we may then expand \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_1 = \sum_{\substack{d_1, d_2, d_\Delta \le x^{\eta} \\ v = (d_1, d_2) = (d_1, d_\Delta) = (d_2, d_\Delta) \\ d_1 d_2 d_\Delta \mid (a_2v)^\infty}} \mathcal{D}_2(d_1, d_2, d_\Delta, v), \end{equation} where \[ \mathcal{D}_2 := \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r, a_1 a_2) = 1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, (a_2 k_2)^\infty) = d_1 \\ (k_2, (a_2 k_1)^\infty) = d_2 \\ (k_1 - k_2, (a_2 k_1 k_2)^\infty) = d_\Delta \\ |k_1 - k_2| > K/x^\eta \\ (k_1 k_2, re) = 1 \\ k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{re}}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a_1 h \frac{\overline{a_2 k_1}}{r} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $v,d_1,d_2,d_\Delta$ and expand (8.4).

nodes.name: Change variables
nodes.statement: Changing variables $k_i \mapsto d_i k_i$, this is the same as the sum \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{D}_2 = \sum_{e \in \mathscr{E}} \sum_{(r, a_1 a_2) = 1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, a_2 d_2 k_2) = 1 \\ (k_2, a_2 d_1 k_1) = 1 \\ (d_1 k_1 - d_2 k_2, (a_2 d_1 d_2 k_1 k_2)^\infty) = d_\Delta \\ |d_1 k_1 - d_2 k_2| > K/x^{\eta} \\ (d_1 k_1 d_2 k_2, re) = 1 \\ d_1 k_1 \equiv d_2 k_2 \pmod{re}}} u_{d_1k_1} \overline{u_{d_2k_2}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a_1 h \frac{\overline{a_2d_1k_1}}{r} \right) \\ = \sum_{\substack{e \in \mathscr{E} \\ (e, d_1 d_2) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{(r, a_1 a_2) = 1 \\ (r, d_1 d_2) = 1}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, k_2) = 1 \\ (k_1 k_2, re a_2 d_1 d_2) = 1 \\ (d_1 k_1 - d_2 k_2, (a_2 d_1 d_2)^\infty) = d_\Delta \\ |d_1 k_1 - d_2 k_2| > K/x^\eta \\ d_1k_1 \equiv d_2k_2 \pmod{re}}} u_{d_1k_1} \overline{u_{d_2k_2}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a_1 h \frac{\overline{a_2d_1k_1}}{r} \right). \end{aligned} \] Let us denote \[ a := a_1 \textnormal{sgn}(a_2) \qquad\qquad \text{and} \qquad\qquad b := |a_2| d_1 \] for convenience; recalling that $d_2 d_\Delta \mid (a_2 v)^\infty \mid b^\infty$, and that we chose $\mathcal{E} = \{e \sim E : e \text{ prime},\ e \nmid a_2\}$ in \cref{eq:averaging-set}, we further get \[ \mathcal{D}_2 = \sum_{\substack{e \sim E \text{ prime} \\ (e, b) = 1}} \sum_{(r, ab) = 1} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, k_2) = 1 \\ (k_1 k_2, re b) = 1 \\ d_1k_1 - d_2k_2 = red_\Delta t \\ (t, b) = 1,\ red_\Delta |t| > K/x^\eta}} u_{d_1k_1} \overline{u_{d_2k_2}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a h \frac{\overline{bk_1}}{r} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $k_i\mapsto d_ik_i$ and set $b$.

nodes.name: Record size of a
nodes.statement: At this point we record that, since $a_1, a_2 \ll x^{\delta} \le x^\eta$ by \cref{eq:conditions}, we have \[ d_1 d_2 d_\Delta \mid b^\infty \qquad\qquad \text{and} \qquad\qquad a b d_1 d_2 d_\Delta v \ll x^{O(\eta)}, \] as needed in \cref{prop:drappeau-expo}.
nodes.statement_short: Record (8.5).

nodes.name: Möbius inversion
nodes.statement: We can also get rid of the restriction $(r, a) = 1$ using M\"obius inversion, by writing $\mathbbm{1}_{(r, a) = 1} = \sum_{d_a \mid a} \mu(d_a) \mathbbm{1}_{d_a \mid r}$ and expanding \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_2(d_1, d_2, d_\Delta, v) = \sum_{d_a \mid a} \mu(d_a)\, \mathcal{D}_3(d_1, d_2, d_\Delta, v, d_a), \end{equation} where \[ \mathcal{D}_3 := \sum_{\substack{e \sim E \text{ prime} \\ (e, b) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{(r, b) = 1 \\ r \equiv 0 \pmod{d_a}}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k_1, k_2) = 1 \\ (k_1 k_2, re b) = 1 \\ d_1k_1 - d_2k_2 = red_\Delta t \\ (t, b) = 1,\ red_\Delta |t| > K/x^\eta}} u_{d_1k_1} \overline{u_{d_2k_2}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a h \frac{\overline{bk_1}}{r} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Remove $(r,a)=1$ by Möbius inversion.

nodes.name: Expand u_k
nodes.statement: Finally, using the definition of $(u_k)_k$ from \cref{eq:u-def} and the fact that $(d_2, k_2) = 1$, we can expand \[ u_{d_2 k_2} = \sum_{\delta_1 \delta_2 = d_2} \sum_{n\ell = k_2} \beta_{\delta_1 n} \gamma_{\delta_2 \ell}, \] and thus \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_3(d_1, d_2, d_\Delta, v, d_a) = \sum_{\delta_1 \delta_2 = d_2} \mathcal{D}_4(d_1, d_2, d_\Delta, v, d_a, \delta_1), \end{equation} where \[ \mathcal{D}_4 := \sum_{\substack{e \sim E \text{ prime} \\ (e, b) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{(r, b) = 1 \\ r \equiv 0 \pmod{d_a}}} \Phi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \frac{1}{r} \sum_{\substack{(k, n\ell) = 1 \\ (k n \ell, re b) = 1 \\ d_1k - d_2n \ell = red_\Delta t \\ (t, b) = 1,\ red_\Delta |t| > K/x^\eta}} u_{d_1k} \overline{\beta_{\delta_1 n} \gamma_{\delta_2 \ell}} \sum_{1 \le |h| \le H} \widehat{\Phi}\left(\frac{hM}{r}\right) \textnormal{e}\left(a h \frac{\overline{bk}}{r} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand $u_{k_2}$ as $\beta*\gamma$, giving (8.6).

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 8.3
nodes.statement: We can now apply \cref{prop:drappeau-expo} for the sequences \[ u'_k := u_{d_1 k}, \qquad\quad \beta'_n := \overline{\beta_{\delta_1 n}}, \qquad\quad \gamma'_\ell := \overline{\gamma_{\delta_2 \ell}}, \] supported in $k \asymp K/d_1$, $n \sim N/\delta_1$, and $\ell \sim L/\delta_2$ respectively, to get \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_4 \ll_{\eta,\varepsilon} x^{O(\eta) - \varepsilon/4} \frac{K^2}{R}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 8.3 to get (8.7).

nodes.name: Combine
